The gap between how much of the cap is in use now and the cap itself.
questions.why: Headroom is defined as the difference between current usage and the quota cap, so it shows how much room remains before a request would be refused.

questions.prompt: A team's project still has ample CPU and disk, yet requests to create new database instances in one region fail with a refusal message. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Network bandwidth is saturated by replication traffic.
The database engine version is out of date.
The project's count of database instances in that region has reached its quota.
Storage on each existing instance is full.
questions.why: A quota rejects requests that would push usage over the cap, and the refusal here points to a count limit being hit even though CPU and storage look normal.

questions.prompt: A quota that a team needs for growth is marked as fixed, and the forecast shows usage will exceed it in six weeks. Which response is right?
choices: Redesign or split the workload so usage stays under the fixed cap, since an increase request cannot raise it.
Set an alert at 90 percent and keep the current design.
Check the monthly bill to see whether the cap can be paid off.
File an increase request now and wait for approval.
questions.why: Some quotas are fixed and cannot be raised at all, so the only real options are to reduce usage or change how the work is divided.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a database team should monitor quotas even when CPU and storage look fine, and name one limit or tradeoff of raising a quota.
lessons.modelAnswer: CPU and storage show how hard the existing instances are working, but a quota is a separate ceiling on how many resources the project may create or use. When usage reaches that ceiling, the provider refuses new instances, connections, or storage, and the failure looks like a create error, not a slow system. So we track usage against each quota, alert well before it is reached, and file increase requests ahead of planned growth. One tradeoff: raising a quota is not free, because higher limits allow more spend and a runaway script can consume more before anyone notices. So the increase should be sized from a forecast, and the alerts should still fire on the new limit.
rubricPoints: A quota is a provider-set cap on a resource type, separate from CPU or storage utilisation.
Exhausted quotas cause refused requests, such as failed creates or connection errors, not gradual slowdown.
Monitor usage against quota and alert before the cap is reached, using headroom.
Raising a quota has a cost tradeoff: higher caps permit higher spend and larger failures.

suggested.rationale: Quota names, limits, and request procedures are catalogue-style facts best learned by reading the quota documentation and checking the console.

lessons.plain: When several parts of a database system want the same limited resource at the same moment, they contend for it, and whoever loses has to wait. Think of a shared kitchen with one oven: if three cooks need it at once, dishes queue and every meal arrives late. Database contention works the same way. The shared resource might be processor time, memory, disk reads and writes, the number of open connections, or a row that one transaction is holding while another needs it. Investigating contention means working out which shared resource is full, which workloads are using it, and whether the slowdown comes from the resource being too small or from one piece of work crowding out the rest. A good investigation finds the cause before anyone buys a bigger machine.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database that was fast last week now has response times that jump every afternoon, while the server's average CPU usage looks only moderately high. Before reading anything, what are two different shared resources that could be the bottleneck, and what would you check first to tell them apart?
lessons.teach:
Resource contention means two or more pieces of work need the same limited resource and must take turns. The main shared resources in a database are CPU, memory (space used to cache data so it does not have to be read from disk), storage I/O (the reads and writes per second that the disks can handle), the connection limit (how many clients may be connected at once), and locks. A lock is a marker one transaction sets on rows or tables so that others must wait until it finishes.

Why it works: a request is only as fast as the longest wait it has to endure. If a query finishes its computation instantly but then waits for a lock held by a long-running transaction, users see slowness even though CPU is idle. So the investigation starts by sorting out the wait: is the work computing, reading from disk, or queuing behind something else?

Worked example: latency doubles at 14:00. Step 1: check the resource graphs for that window. CPU is at 55 percent, but disk I/O is at 98 percent of its provisioned limit. Step 2: list the queries active during that window. A nightly reporting scan reads most of a large table, and it now runs at 14:00 because a schedule was changed. Step 3: confirm the link by checking that latency recovers when the report is paused. The cause is I/O contention from one workload, not an undersized instance.

Common mistake: reading moderate average CPU as proof the server is fine, or reading high average CPU as proof it needs a bigger size. Averages hide short spikes, and resizing may only hide the symptom while the report still competes with live traffic.

In a running system, contention shows up as timeouts, connection pool exhaustion (new requests cannot obtain a connection and fail), and retries that add even more load to the saturated resource. The fastest route to the cause is to match the slowdown to the resource that is saturated at the same moment, then to the workload using that resource.

questions.prompt: A parcel-tracking company's update API starts timing out at 07:15 each weekday. Step 1: the database's CPU sits at 22 percent and disk I/O at 40 percent of their limits, so neither is saturated. Step 2: the open connections count is 1,000 out of a 1,000 limit, and the application's connection pool reports that new requests cannot obtain a connection. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: once that workload is stopped, the connection count drops and the timeouts stop.
choices: Double the number of vCPUs on the database so it can serve more connections at once.
Raise the connection limit to 2,000 and restart the update API so the pool resets.
Compare the average CPU over the previous week to see whether usage has been trending upward.
Group the open sessions by client application to find which workload is holding the connections.
questions.why: The connection limit is the saturated resource at the time of the timeouts, so the next step is to identify the workload that holds those connections, which is what grouping sessions by client does.

questions.prompt: A query finishes its computation almost immediately but still takes several seconds to return. Monitoring shows CPU idle and disk I/O low. Which kind of contention is the most likely cause?
choices: A lock held by another transaction that the query must wait for.
Storage I/O saturation, because the disks cannot keep up with writes.
Memory exhaustion, because the query's result set is too large to cache.
Connection pool exhaustion, because the application is sending too many queries.
questions.why: When computation and disk activity are low but the request is still slow, the wait is most likely a lock set by another transaction that blocks the query until it finishes.

questions.prompt: A team reviewing a reporting replica sees average CPU of 32 percent across the day and concludes the server has spare capacity. Users report slow pages every afternoon. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: The replica must be undersized, so the team should move to a larger machine type immediately.
Averages can hide short spikes, so the afternoon peaks should be checked in the time window where pages are slow.
Average CPU is reliable, so the slow pages must come from the application code, not the database.
Low average CPU proves that no shared resource is contended, so the connection limit can be ignored.
questions.why: An average over the whole day can conceal short saturation spikes, so the investigation should examine the resource graphs for the exact afternoon window when pages slow down.

questions.prompt: A service's database connection pool is exhausted during a traffic peak. Each client that receives a failure immediately retries its request in a tight loop with no delay. What is the most appropriate change to reduce the contention?
choices: Add a spacing delay that grows between retries and cap the total number of attempts.
Restart the database each time the pool reports exhaustion to clear the waiting requests.
Remove the connection pool so every request opens its own connection right away.
Increase the number of retries so that every failed request eventually succeeds.
questions.why: Immediate, unlimited retries add load to a resource that is already saturated, so spacing retries out with backoff and capping attempts reduces the extra pressure on the connection limit.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would investigate a database that is slow only during business hours, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by deciding whether the slowness is waiting or working. I would compare the peak-hour graphs for CPU, memory, disk I/O and connection count against the quiet hours, looking for a resource at or near its limit at the same time as the latency spike. Next I would list what was running during that window, grouped by client or job, to see which workload is using the saturated resource. If the wait is on locks instead, I would look for long-open transactions. Once I have a suspect, I would test it, for example by pausing that job and checking whether latency recovers. A limit of this approach is that it depends on the monitoring data capturing the spike; averages over coarse time windows can hide a short burst, so I would look at finer granularity. Resizing is only the right answer after I have shown the bottleneck is a genuine capacity shortage rather than one workload crowding out the others.
rubricPoints: Separate waiting on locks or connections from waiting on CPU, memory or I/O before acting.
Correlate the slowdown with the resource that is saturated during the same window.
Identify which workload or client is consuming the contended resource.
Name a limit, such as averages hiding spikes or monitoring gaps, and avoid resizing as the first fix.

suggested.rationale: Investigating contention is mainly about reasoning from symptoms to the saturated resource and workload, which an exam-style situation exercises better than a single listed mission.

lessons.plain: Setting up alerts means telling a monitoring system to watch a number about your database, such as how many errors happen or how long queries take, and to notify a person when that number stays past a limit you chose. Think of a smoke detector: it does not put out the fire, but it wakes someone before the house is lost. A good alert stays quiet when things are fine, fires when a real problem starts, and tells the responder what to look at first. Designing one means picking the right signal, the right limit, and how long the limit must be crossed before anyone is notified.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database has a rule that pages you whenever a single error is logged. Why might this be a bad idea, and what single change would make it better?
lessons.teach:
An alert is a rule that watches a metric. A metric is a number recorded over time, such as the count of failed connections per minute or the 95th percentile query latency, meaning the response time that 95 percent of queries beat. An alerting policy holds one or more conditions. Each condition has a threshold (the limit), a comparison (above or below), and a duration (how long the value must stay past the limit before the rule fires). When it fires, the policy sends a notification through a channel such as email or a paging tool, and it can carry documentation that tells the responder what to check first.

Why the duration matters: a single sample can spike for reasons that do not matter. Requiring the value to stay high for, say, ten minutes filters out noise and prevents alerts that open and close repeatedly.

Worked example: you watch database CPU utilization with a threshold of 80 percent, condition above, duration 10 minutes. At 09:00 CPU reads 85, 88 and 90 at three one-minute samples, then drops to 60. Only three consecutive minutes are above the threshold, fewer than ten, so no alert fires. At 09:20 CPU stays above 80 for ten consecutive minutes, so the policy fires once and sends one notification.

Common mistake: alerting on a metric with no duration, or choosing a threshold by guesswork. Both produce either floods of pages or silence during real trouble, and responders learn to ignore the channel.

Consequence: if the error-rate or replication-lag alert never fires, an outage can run for hours before a user reports it. If every minor blip pages someone at night, the team stops trusting alerts altogether. An error alert should watch the rate of errors rather than a raw total that only grows, and a performance alert should name the user impact it protects.

questions.prompt: A team wants an alert for a reporting database whose error counter only ever goes up. Readings: 1200 at 10:00, 1215 at 10:01, 1231 at 10:02, 1240 at 10:03. The alert rule is: threshold 12 errors per minute, condition above, duration 3 minutes. Step 1 turns the rising counter into a per-minute rate by subtracting each reading from the next, giving 15, 16 and 9 errors per minute for 10:01, 10:02 and 10:03. Step 2 compares each per-minute rate with 12 and marks it above or not: above, above, not above. Step 3 is missing. What should step 3 conclude?
choices: The average of the three rates is above 12, so the alert fires at 10:02.
The total of 51 errors since 10:00 is above 12, so the alert fires at 10:03.
Two minutes above the threshold is enough, so the alert fires at 10:02 and then closes at 10:03.
The longest run above 12 is only two minutes (10:01 and 10:02), because the 9 at 10:03 breaks it, so the 3-minute duration is not met and no alert fires.
questions.why: The duration requires the value to stay past the threshold for consecutive minutes, and the 9 at 10:03 breaks the run at two minutes, so the rule does not fire.

questions.prompt: A replica lag alert has a threshold of 30 seconds, condition above, and duration 0 seconds. Why is this setup likely to cause trouble?
choices: The comparison should be below, not above, so zero duration makes the alert fire when lag is healthy.
Lag is not a metric, so no threshold can be attached to it at all.
Zero duration means the alert can never fire, because lag must be held for a time before it counts.
A brief single-sample spike past 30 seconds fires the rule immediately, so the alert can open and close repeatedly and teach the team to ignore it.
questions.why: Without a duration, one sample past the limit fires the policy, which creates noise that trains responders to ignore alerts.

questions.prompt: A team sets an error alert on a running total of failed logins that has reached 500 and keeps rising. The rule is: total above 500. Why is this a poor design for detecting new trouble?
choices: The alert will fire every minute because the total increases every minute.
A total can only be compared below a threshold, so this comparison is invalid.
Once the total passes 500 it stays above it forever, so the alert gives no signal about whether failures are happening now; a rate of failures per minute would show current trouble.
Totals are not allowed as metrics, so the rule will be rejected when saved.
questions.why: A raw total that only grows stays past any fixed limit once crossed, so an error alert should watch the rate of errors instead.

questions.prompt: Which performance alert best names the user impact it protects?
choices: Disk usage above 70 percent for 15 minutes on the analytics volume.
Connection pool count above 40 for 5 minutes on the staging cluster.
Backup job duration above 2 hours on the nightly archive.
Checkout query 95th percentile latency above 800 ms for 5 minutes, so shoppers do not wait long to pay.
questions.why: The correct option pairs a latency metric with a stated duration and a clear user effect, while the others describe resource levels without naming who is harmed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up an alert on database errors and an alert on slow queries, naming one limit or tradeoff in your choice of threshold and duration.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from what users feel. For errors I would alert on the rate of failed requests divided by total requests, not the raw count, because the raw count grows all day and tells you nothing about health. I would set the threshold above normal daily noise, measured over the past few weeks, and require it to hold for several minutes so a brief blip does not page anyone. For slow queries I would watch a high percentile of query latency, such as the 95th, against the target the service promises. The tradeoff is that a longer duration and a higher threshold mean fewer false pages but a slower warning, so a real outage can run longer before anyone is told. I would accept a few minutes of delay in exchange for fewer false alarms, and I would add a short note to the policy saying which dashboard and runbook to open first.
rubricPoints: Alert on a rate or a high percentile rather than a raw total or an average that hides spikes
Set the threshold from normal baseline behaviour, not a guess
Use a duration so brief blips do not page anyone
Name the tradeoff: longer duration and higher threshold cut false alarms but delay warning of real problems

suggested.rationale: The planned metric alarm builder engine would let the learner set thresholds, durations and conditions and see which alerts would fire against a sample metric stream.

lessons.plain: A backup is a saved copy of your data, taken at a moment in time and kept apart from the live system, so you can get it back after something goes wrong, such as an accidental delete, a bad release, or a failed disk. Recovery is the work of putting that copy back into service. Managed database services can take these copies on a schedule for you, so nobody has to remember to do it. The real skill is choosing how often copies are taken, how long they are kept, and how far back you can go, because those choices decide how much data you could lose and how long you would be offline.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database is backed up automatically every night at 02:00. At 14:30 someone accidentally deletes a table. Roughly how much of the data written that day could you lose if you restored last night's copy, and what would you need to know to reduce that loss?
lessons.teach:
A backup is a copy of a database taken at a point in time and stored separately from the live system. An automated scheduled backup is one the managed service takes on its own, at a time window you choose, and keeps for a retention period, meaning the number of copies or days before old ones are deleted. An on-demand backup is one you trigger yourself, for example just before a risky change. Point-in-time recovery, often shortened to PITR, is a feature that keeps a continuous log of changes so the database can be rebuilt to almost any moment inside the retention window, not just to a scheduled snapshot. Two terms matter for every choice: the recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data loss you can accept, measured as time, and the recovery time objective (RTO) is how long you can be offline while recovering.

Worked example. A database takes a full backup daily at 02:00 and has point-in-time recovery turned on. At 14:30 a migration drops a table. Step 1: the newest scheduled copy is from 02:00, so about 12.5 hours of writes exist only in the live database. Step 2: restoring that copy would bring the table back but lose those hours. Step 3: with PITR, the service replays its change log up to 14:29, so only the seconds before the mistake are lost. Step 4: you restore into a new instance, check row counts, and then repoint the application, and that repointing time counts against your RTO.

Common mistake: treating 'automatic backups are on' as 'we are protected'. Nobody has tested a restore, retention may have already deleted the copy from before the bad change, or the copies sit in the same region as the failure.

Consequence: the gap between the last good recovery point and the failure sets your data loss, and the restore duration plus repointing sets your downtime. A backup you have never restored is a guess about both numbers.

questions.prompt: A clinic's scheduling database takes a full backup every Sunday at 23:00, keeps backups for 14 days, and has point-in-time recovery (PITR) turned on. On Thursday at 09:15 a maintenance script wrongly overwrites appointment times for every patient. Step 1: the newest scheduled full copy is from the previous Sunday, so restoring it alone would lose several days of bookings. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: restore that moment into a new instance, check appointment counts and sample records, then repoint the scheduling application, counting the repointing time against the recovery time objective.
choices: Restore the Sunday 23:00 full backup into the original instance, since it is the newest copy that exists.
Choose a recovery time of 09:14, just before the script ran, as the target for a PITR restore.
Turn on point-in-time recovery now, so the change log starts covering the overwrite that already happened.
Extend the retention period to 30 days so that older copies are kept for a later restore.
questions.why: The missing step is picking the exact target moment just before the bad change, which lets PITR replay the log up to that point and lose only the seconds before the mistake.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between an automated scheduled backup and an on-demand backup?
choices: A scheduled backup is taken by the managed service at a window you set and kept for a retention period, while an on-demand backup is triggered by you whenever you choose.
A scheduled backup can only restore the whole database, while an on-demand backup can restore a single table.
A scheduled backup is triggered by you before a risky change, while an on-demand backup runs at a fixed time.
A scheduled backup is kept forever, while an on-demand backup is deleted after one day.
questions.why: Scheduled backups run automatically in a chosen time window and expire under retention, while on-demand backups are started by a person at a moment they pick.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm takes nightly backups that are kept for 7 days, with point-in-time recovery turned off. A data error that began 10 days ago is only discovered today. Which statement is correct?
choices: Copies from before the error may already have been deleted by retention, and without PITR the firm can only restore to a scheduled copy that still exists.
The firm can recover to the exact moment the error began, since the backup service keeps a log by default.
The firm can recover to any moment in the last 10 days because nightly backups cover that period.
The firm can recover to any moment in the last 7 days, so the error is fully recoverable to just before it started.
questions.why: Retention deletes old copies, and without PITR there is no continuous log, so recovery is limited to whichever scheduled copies remain.

questions.prompt: An online game studio's database restore takes 95 minutes, and repointing the game servers to the restored instance takes 20 minutes. If the database is offline from the moment of failure until the game is back on the new instance, how long is the downtime that counts against the recovery time objective (RTO)?
choices: 20 minutes, because repointing is the only step that is measured against the RTO.
95 minutes, because only the restore time counts against the RTO.
115 minutes, because the restore and the repointing both add to the time the game is offline.
About 75 minutes, which is the average of the two steps.
questions.why: Downtime is the total time offline, so the restore duration and the repointing duration add together to give the RTO that is actually experienced.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how scheduled automatic backups differ from point-in-time recovery, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying only on daily scheduled backups.
lessons.modelAnswer: A scheduled automatic backup is a full copy the service takes at a set time, such as every night, and keeps for a retention period. Point-in-time recovery is different: the service also keeps a continuous log of changes, so we can rebuild the database to a chosen moment, like a few seconds before a bad migration, as long as that moment is inside the retention window. The main limit of relying only on daily backups is data loss. If the failure happens at 14:30, a 02:00 copy loses about twelve and a half hours of writes, which may break our recovery point objective. The tradeoff is cost and complexity: PITR adds storage for logs and needs a restore to a new instance, so we also have to budget time for restore and repointing against our recovery time objective, and test it regularly.
rubricPoints: Scheduled backups are full copies taken at set times and kept for a retention period
Point-in-time recovery uses continuous change logs to restore to a chosen moment
Daily-only backups can lose many hours of writes after a failure
Recovery has a cost in storage and a time cost in restoring and repointing applications
A restore should be tested, because an untested backup is not proven

suggested.rationale: Choosing a backup plan for a failure scenario needs reasoning about RPO, retention, and restore time, which an exam-style situation practises better than reading settings alone.

lessons.plain: Exporting a database means copying its contents out into a file kept somewhere safe, and importing means loading such a file back into a database. Think of it like photocopying a filing cabinet into a box so you can move the cabinet, share its contents, or rebuild it elsewhere. The file can hold the table definitions and the rows, usually as a set of SQL statements or as plain comma-separated values. Configuring the job means choosing what to copy, where the file lands, and which identities may write and read it. Done carelessly, the copy can be inconsistent or the restore can fail, so the details matter.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you export a shop's orders table on Monday to a file, then import that file into a brand-new empty database on Friday. What could differ between the original data and the restored data, and what would cause the difference?
lessons.teach:
An export is a logical copy of a database: the service reads the schema (the table structures) and the rows, then writes them to a file, often called a dump. An import is the reverse: a new or existing database reads that file and recreates the structures and rows. The file usually lives in object storage, which is a cloud service that keeps named files in containers called buckets. The database service does not use your personal login to write there; it uses a service identity, meaning a machine account that needs its own write permission on the bucket for an export and read permission for an import. A consistent export means every table is read as of one single moment, so a related pair like orders and order_items agree with each other. Without that, the file can contain an order whose line items were written after the copy passed them.

Worked example: you export a database with tables orders and order_items to a bucket in the same region as the database. Step one, you choose the database, or only specific tables if you want a partial copy. Step two, the service reads both tables as of one moment. Step three, it writes the file into the bucket. Step four, you create an empty target database running a compatible version and grant its import identity read access to the file. Step five, the import recreates the tables and loads the rows. If the target already contains rows with the same primary keys, the load fails on duplicates.

A common mistake is treating an export as a continuous backup that restores to any second. An export is a snapshot from one moment, so anything written after that moment is not in the file. Another mistake is importing into a database that already holds conflicting data. In a running system, a large export reads heavily from the live database, so CPU and disk input and output on the primary can rise and slow user queries while the job runs.

questions.prompt: A freight company, Harbor Lane Logistics, exports two tables, shipments and parcel_scans, from its operations database into a bucket named hl-dumps in the same region. The sequence is: step 1, choose the two tables for the export. Step 2, grant the database's service identity write permission on the hl-dumps bucket. Step 3, [missing step]. Step 4, the export file sits in hl-dumps, and a separate target database is created with an import identity that has read access to that file. Which step belongs in the blank?
choices: The service reads shipments and parcel_scans as of one single moment and writes them into the file in the bucket.
The company's personal login writes the file into the bucket, so the service identity is not needed.
Each table is exported on its own schedule, so shipments and parcel_scans are copied at different times.
The target database runs the import before the export has started, so the file is read first.
questions.why: The export must read both related tables as of one moment and then write that file to the bucket, which is the step that turns the chosen tables into the file that step 4 refers to.

questions.prompt: A database service needs to write an export file into a storage bucket. Which statement correctly describes the identity it uses?
choices: It uses anonymous access, so the bucket must be made public before the export runs.
It uses a machine account called a service identity, which needs its own write permission on the bucket.
It uses the administrator's personal login, so no extra permission is needed on the bucket.
It uses the bucket's own owner account, so the database itself needs no identity.
questions.why: The database service writes using a dedicated machine account, which must be granted write permission on the bucket for an export to succeed.

questions.prompt: A payments team exports a ledger database with tables accounts and transfers. Which kind of export keeps each transfer consistent with the account rows it refers to?
choices: An export that skips transfers and copies only accounts, so no references can disagree.
An export that reads accounts in the morning and transfers in the afternoon.
An export that reads the rows of each table at whatever time its reader reaches them.
An export that reads every table as of one single moment, so the two tables agree with each other.
questions.why: A consistent export reads all related tables as of one moment, so the copied transfers and accounts match, which is the only option that describes this.

questions.prompt: A team takes an export of its order database at 02:00 and needs to restore the data as it stood at 14:37 the same day. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The export can restore any second between 02:00 and 14:37 because it is a continuous backup.
The export can restore 14:37 if the file is stored in a bucket in the same region as the database.
The export cannot give the 14:37 state, because it is a snapshot from one moment and holds nothing written after 02:00.
The export can be used only if the team also imports the file twice, once at 02:00 and again at 14:37.
questions.why: An export is a snapshot from a single moment, so it does not contain changes made after that moment and cannot restore an arbitrary later second.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would configure an export of a production database so it can be imported into a new test environment. Name one limit or tradeoff of the export approach you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would export the production database to a bucket in the same region, using a dedicated service identity that can only write to that one bucket. I would confirm the export is consistent, so related tables are captured at the same moment. Then I would create an empty target in the test environment running a compatible version, grant its import identity read access to the file, and import. The main tradeoff is that an export is a snapshot. Anything written after it started is missing from the test copy, so the test data is only as current as that moment. It also reads heavily from production while running, so I would check that CPU and disk load stay acceptable before starting. For a fresh restore point I would want a proper backup approach instead of relying on this file.
rubricPoints: An export is a logical copy taken at one moment, so later writes are not included.
Consistency matters so related tables agree with each other in the file.
The service identity needs explicit write (export) or read (import) permission on the storage location.
Importing into a non-empty database with conflicting keys fails, and a large export adds load to the live database.

suggested.rationale: The SQL lab could have you dump a small database to a file and load it into an empty copy, which practises the export and import steps directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine a fire destroys your filing cabinet. Two questions decide how you prepare. First, how long can the office run without its files before the business suffers? Second, how much recent work can you afford to lose, measured as the gap between the last saved copy and the moment of the fire? Those two answers are the recovery time objective and the recovery point objective. Point-in-time recovery is a method that rebuilds data as it looked at any chosen moment, not just at the last full copy. Designing for these means choosing backup frequency, change logs and restore steps that meet the numbers the business actually agreed to.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database is backed up every night at 02:00. At 14:37 a faulty script deletes a table. Without any further information, what is the most recent state you could safely return to, and roughly how much work would be lost?
lessons.teach:
Recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest acceptable time between a failure and the moment service works again. Recovery point objective (RPO) is the longest acceptable span of data you can lose, measured backwards from the failure to the last recoverable change. Both are targets set by the business, and the engineer designs backups and restore steps to meet them.

Point-in-time recovery (PITR) is the ability to restore a database to a chosen moment, such as 14:36:00. It works by combining a base backup with a continuous change log, which records every committed write in order. You restore the base backup, then replay the log up to the target moment. Without the log, you can only return to the moments when backups were taken.

Worked example. Full backups run at 02:00 daily. Change logs are kept for seven days. At 14:37 a faulty job deletes rows from the rides table. Step one: choose a target of 14:36, just before the damage. Step two: restore the 02:00 backup to a new instance, which takes about 40 minutes, so the RTO is roughly that plus checks. Step three: replay the logs from 02:00 to 14:36. Only changes made between 14:36 and 14:37 are lost, so the achieved RPO is about one minute, even though full backups are daily.

Common mistake: treating the backup schedule as the RPO. A daily backup alone allows up to 24 hours of loss. The change log is what shrinks the RPO. Another mistake is never timing a real restore, which leaves the RTO as a guess.

In a running system, nightly backups alone would have erased about twelve hours of completed rides in this incident, and the team would have discovered the true restore duration only during the outage. Designing for RTO and RPO means writing both numbers down and proving them with a timed restore test.

questions.prompt: SeatHop, a ticketing company, takes a full backup every Sunday at 01:00 and keeps its change log (the ordered record of every committed write, which makes point-in-time recovery possible) for 14 days. On Wednesday at 10:20 a migration script accidentally overwrites the seats table. The on-call engineer follows these steps. Step one: choose a recovery target of 10:19:00, just before the bad write. Step two: restore the Sunday 01:00 backup to a new instance, which takes about 55 minutes. Step three is missing from the runbook. Which completion correctly finishes the procedure?
choices: Replay the change log from the Sunday backup up to 10:20:30 so that the bad write is included and then verified.
Delete the change log entries after 10:19:00 to save storage before the restored copy is checked.
Skip the change log and promote the restored Sunday backup as the live database, since it is the most recent full copy.
Replay the change log from the Sunday 01:00 backup moment forward and stop at 10:19:00, so the bad write is excluded.
questions.why: Replaying the log from the backup moment and stopping at the chosen target rebuilds the database as it was just before the damage, which is the purpose of point-in-time recovery.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does recovery point objective (RPO, the longest acceptable span of data you can lose before a failure) describe?
choices: The longest acceptable time between a failure and the moment service works again.
The number of backup copies that must be stored in a second region.
The time it takes to copy a backup from one storage bucket to another.
The longest acceptable span of recent data loss, measured backwards from the failure to the last recoverable change.
questions.why: RPO measures how much recent data could be lost, counted backwards from the failure to the last change that can be recovered.

questions.prompt: A small analytics service takes a full backup every six hours and keeps no change log. A failure happens just before the next backup is due. What is the worst-case RPO for this service?
choices: About 3 hours, because the average backup age is half the interval.
About 6 hours, because the service can only return to the last backup point.
Zero, because the most recent backup is always complete.
About 15 minutes, because backups run often enough to limit loss.
questions.why: With no change log, the only recoverable points are the backup moments, so the data written since the last backup, up to six hours, can be lost.

questions.prompt: A team measures a test restore of a 300 GB backup and it takes 90 minutes. They want to state their RTO. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Their RTO is zero, because having a backup means service can resume immediately.
Their RTO is about 90 minutes plus time to verify the restored data and switch traffic to it.
Their RTO equals how often they run backups, so it depends on the schedule rather than the restore.
Their RTO is 90 minutes regardless of how much data changed since the backup was taken.
questions.why: RTO is the full time from failure until service works, so the timed restore must be extended by the checks and cutover steps needed before users are served again.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only ever restored from a nightly backup what RTO and RPO mean, how point-in-time recovery changes the picture, and one limit or tradeoff of adding it.
lessons.modelAnswer: RTO is how long we can be down after a failure before service must be back. RPO is how much recent data we can afford to lose, counted back from the failure. A nightly backup alone gives an RPO of up to a day, because everything since the last copy is gone. Point-in-time recovery adds a continuous change log on top of a base backup, so we can rebuild the data at a chosen moment, such as just before a bad delete. That can bring the RPO down to minutes. The tradeoff is cost and complexity: the logs take storage and must be kept long enough to cover the recovery window, and replaying them takes time, so the RTO can grow as the log gets longer. We also need to test a real restore, because the RTO we promise is only what we have actually timed.
rubricPoints: RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime after a failure.
RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured back from the failure.
A backup schedule alone sets the RPO; a continuous change log lets point-in-time recovery shrink it.
Point-in-time recovery needs log retention and replay time, which affect cost and RTO, and restores must be tested.

suggested.rationale: The disaster-recovery planner engine would let the learner set RTO and RPO targets and check whether a backup and log schedule meets them, which no current mission covers.

lessons.plain: A data retention policy is the written rule that says how long a kind of data must be kept and what happens when that time is up. Think of a library that keeps tax records for seven years, keeps new magazines for a month, and shreds old receipts after a year. Each kind of data gets its own clock. When the clock runs out, the data is deleted or moved to cheaper storage. Engineers set these rules so the database does not grow forever, the company meets its legal duties, and private information is not kept longer than needed. The rule only works if something enforces it on a schedule.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer asks you to delete their order history after five years, but finance says invoices must be kept for seven years. Before deleting anything, what would you need to know, and why could deleting the wrong rows be hard to undo?
lessons.teach:
A retention period is the length of time a piece of data must be kept before it can be removed. A retention policy is the set of retention periods for each kind of data, plus the action taken at the end of each period: delete, archive, or hold. Retention rules come from three places: business need (keep orders for reporting), legal or regulatory duty (keep invoices for seven years), and cost or privacy (do not keep personal data longer than needed).

In a database, retention is enforced in several layers. Rows can carry an expiry, often called a TTL (time to live), so the database or a scheduled job removes rows older than a cutoff. Backups and exported files have their own retention settings, which decide how many old copies remain. Logs have another clock. A legal hold is a flag that suspends deletion for specific records while a dispute or investigation is open, even if their period has ended.

Worked example: a telemetry table holds vehicle position readings with a 90-day retention period, and today is 1 June. Step 1: compute the cutoff, which is 3 March (90 days earlier). Step 2: a scheduled job deletes rows whose timestamp is before 3 March. Step 3: a reading from 2 March is removed, and a reading from 4 March stays. Step 4: if one vehicle is under a legal hold, the job must skip its rows even though they are past the cutoff.

Common mistake: setting retention on the live table but forgetting that backups and exports still hold the deleted data for their own period. Deleted data can still exist in those copies, so a retention policy must cover every place the data lives. If the purge job never runs, the table keeps growing until storage and query times suffer, and the business keeps data it promised to delete.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy keeps refill-log rows for 120 days, and today is 10 July. Step 1: the cutoff is 12 March. Step 2: the purge job deletes rows dated before 12 March. Step 3: a row dated 11 March is past the cutoff, so the job removes it. Step 4 is missing: one patient's refill rows fall under a legal hold because a recall investigation is still open. What must the job do with those rows?
choices: The job deletes them, because a legal hold only changes the retention period for rows written after the hold starts
The job skips them while the hold stays open, so they remain even though they are past the cutoff
The job restarts their 120-day period from today so they are kept for another full term
The job deletes them only after the backup copies of the same rows have been checked
questions.why: A legal hold suspends deletion for the specific records it covers while the dispute or investigation is open, even when their retention period has already ended.

questions.prompt: Which option best describes a retention policy as the teaching text uses the term?
choices: The schedule on which database backups are taken each night
Retention periods for each kind of data, each with an end action
A single number of days after which a table's rows expire
A rule that limits which user accounts may read a table
questions.why: A retention policy is the set of retention periods for each kind of data together with the action (delete, archive, or hold) taken when each period ends.

questions.prompt: A support platform sets a 45-day expiry on ticket rows in its live table but keeps nightly backups for 400 days. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Table expiry automatically shortens the backup retention to 45 days, so the backups never hold old tickets
Tickets older than 45 days can still be restored from backups until those backups expire, so the policy does not yet cover every copy
Deleted tickets are fully gone once the 45-day expiry runs, because the live table is the only place they are stored
Backups are unaffected by table expiry, so the team must delete the backup files by hand every day
questions.why: A row-level expiry only removes the live copy, and the backups keep their own retention clock, so the old data can still exist in them until the backup period ends.

questions.prompt: A bookings table keeps rows for 365 days. A purge job runs on 14 October 2025. Which row should the job delete?
choices: A booking dated 14 October 2024
A booking dated 1 October 2025
A booking dated 20 October 2024
A booking dated 13 October 2024
questions.why: The cutoff is 14 October 2024 (365 days before 14 October 2025, with no leap day in between), and rows dated before the cutoff are past their period, so the 13 October 2024 booking is the only one removed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a data retention policy differs from a backup schedule, and name one limit or tradeoff of setting retention too short or too long.
lessons.modelAnswer: A retention policy says how long a kind of data must exist and what happens when that time is up. A backup schedule says when copies are taken. They interact: a backup taken today still contains rows the live table deleted last week, so deleted data lives on until backup retention ends. If I set live-table retention to 30 days but backups keep 365 days, a customer's data I was supposed to purge is still recoverable for a year, which may break a privacy promise. The tradeoff runs both ways. Keep retention too short and we may delete records we are legally required to keep, or lose the ability to recover after a bad delete. Keep it too long and storage costs rise, queries slow down, and we hold personal data longer than we need. So the rule should be set by the legal and business owners, enforced by a scheduled job, and checked across backups and exports, not only the live table.
rubricPoints: A retention policy sets how long each kind of data is kept and the action taken at expiry.
Backups and exports keep copies on their own clocks, so deleting from the live table is not the whole story.
Retention set too short risks losing required data; set too long raises cost and privacy exposure.
A legal hold can suspend deletion for specific records even after their retention period has ended.

suggested.rationale: A SQL lab can have the learner write and check a purge query that respects a cutoff and a legal-hold flag, which is where this objective is practised.

lessons.plain: Scaling a database means giving it more capacity when the workload grows. Scaling up, also called vertical scaling, means making one machine bigger with more CPU, more memory, or faster disks. Scaling out, also called horizontal scaling, means adding more machines and spreading the work or the data across them. Choosing between them is an assessment: you look at what is actually the bottleneck, how much downtime you can accept, whether the data can be split across machines without breaking its rules, and what each option costs. A bigger single machine is simpler but has a ceiling and remains a single point of failure. Several machines can go further but need extra coordination work.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your single database server's CPU sits at 100 percent during peak hours, and all the data fits comfortably on one disk. Would you make that server bigger or add a second server to share the load, and why?
lessons.teach:
Scaling up (vertical scaling) means giving one database server more resources: more CPU cores, more memory, or faster storage. Scaling out (horizontal scaling) means adding more servers and dividing the work between them. Assessing the two starts with finding the bottleneck, the resource that actually limits the workload, such as CPU, memory, disk input and output, or many requests fighting over the same record. Scale-up works because one server keeps all data and transactions in one place, so the database stays consistent without coordination. Its weakness is a hardware ceiling, and one failure takes everything down. Scale-out raises the ceiling in two main ways. Read replicas are copies of the data that answer read requests, leaving the main server free for writes. Sharding places different slices of the data on different servers. Scale-out works best when the workload can be divided, and it costs coordination: a query or transaction that touches data on several machines is slower and can fail if one machine is unreachable.

Worked example: a reporting database on a 4-core server runs at 95 percent CPU every evening. Step 1: confirm the bottleneck is CPU during read queries, not disk or locking. Step 2: check the largest machine size available. Doubling to 8 cores costs little engineering effort and is the cheapest first move. Step 3: if reads keep growing, add read replicas so reports run against copies. Step 4: keep the data in one logical database, because splitting it would force the nightly joins to cross machines.

Common mistake: adding servers when the real limit is one hot row that every request updates. More machines do not help, because only one transaction can change that row at a time.

Consequence: once data is sharded, a report that joins two shards must move data between machines, so latency rises, and if one shard is unreachable the whole report fails.

The right choice is the one that removes the actual bottleneck with the least added coordination.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs its shipment-tracking database on a 16-core server, the largest size its provider offers. Each weekday afternoon, driver-app reads push CPU to 92 percent, while disk input and output and lock waits stay low. Step 1: confirm that CPU during read queries is the bottleneck. Step 2: confirm that 16 cores is the largest available size, so adding more cores to this server is not an option. Step 3: missing. Step 4: keep all shipment data in one logical database, because splitting it would force dispatch reports that join tables to cross machines. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Add read replicas so driver-app reads run against copies while the primary server handles writes
Add a second primary server that accepts writes so both primaries share the workload equally
Shard the shipment table by customer ID across four servers so each server carries less of the load
Restart the server each afternoon so the CPU load resets before the driver-app peak
questions.why: With the machine already at its size ceiling and the load coming from reads, read replicas take those reads off the primary while keeping the data in one logical database, as Step 4 requires.

questions.prompt: A small team runs its customer-contacts database on one virtual machine. Queries are slow because the disk cannot keep up with input and output requests, while CPU and memory are mostly idle. Which first move is a scale-up option that targets the actual bottleneck?
choices: Add read replicas so the contact searches run against copies
Move the database to a virtual machine with faster storage, keeping one server
Add three more virtual machines and split the contacts by region
Shard the contacts by last name across two servers
questions.why: Scale-up means giving one server more resources, and faster storage addresses a disk input and output bottleneck while keeping all data on one server with no added coordination.

questions.prompt: A reporting job joins customer records that a team has sharded across three database servers. One night one shard becomes unreachable, and the whole report fails even though two of the three shards are healthy. What explains this outcome?
choices: Scale-out makes queries that span several machines depend on every involved machine being reachable
Sharding removes all coordination, so a shard outage should not affect any query
The report used read replicas, which always fail when any copy is offline
Scale-up servers were used, so a single disk failure stopped the whole job
questions.why: A query or transaction that touches data on several machines needs all of them to respond, which is the coordination cost of scale-out and why one unreachable shard can fail the whole report.

questions.prompt: A sensor-data database receives about 50,000 writes per second from devices, and each device's readings can be stored independently of the others. Dashboards read only the last hour of data for one device at a time. The single server's write throughput is the clear limit. Which approach best removes that bottleneck with the least added coordination?
choices: Upgrade the server to more memory and keep one copy of all readings
Shard the readings by device ID so each dashboard query touches one server
Split each device's readings into hourly tables stored on one server
Add read replicas of the full dataset so dashboards read from copies
questions.why: Because the write load divides cleanly by device and each dashboard query needs only one device's data, sharding by device ID spreads writes across servers while keeping most queries on a single machine.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should add three more database servers because the application is slow. Explain to them when scaling out helps, when scaling up is the better first move, and one limit of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before adding servers, I would check what is actually slow. If the database is CPU-bound on one large workload, a bigger machine is usually the simpler first move: it keeps all data in one place, so transactions stay simple and consistent, and it needs no changes to the application. Its limit is the largest machine you can buy, and it is still one server, so a failure takes it down. Scaling out helps when the work can be split: read replicas take read traffic away from the primary, and sharding spreads data across servers. Its limit is coordination. Any query or transaction that spans several machines gets slower and can fail when one of them is unavailable. If the slowness comes from a single hot row or a lock, extra servers will not help at all. So I would measure the bottleneck first, then choose.
rubricPoints: Scale-up adds resources to one machine and keeps data and transactions simple, but has a hardware ceiling and a single point of failure.
Scale-out adds machines through read replicas or sharding, and suits workloads that can be divided.
Scale-out adds coordination cost, so cross-machine queries and transactions are slower and more failure-prone.
The decision starts with identifying the real bottleneck, since extra machines do not fix contention on one hot record.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between scale-up and scale-out is best practised by reasoning through a realistic bottleneck scenario and then explaining the choice.

lessons.plain: A database instance is the running server that holds your data and answers requests. Scaling it means changing how much work it can handle: giving it more processing power, more memory, more disk space, or faster disk access. Scaling against current workload means matching the size to what the database uses today. Scaling against upcoming workload means making the change before a known busy period, such as a sales event or a seasonal peak, so the database does not slow down or fail when demand arrives. The skill is sizing with a sensible margin, not guessing and not paying for capacity that sits idle.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database runs comfortably on most days but becomes very slow every Monday morning. Before changing anything, what would you measure first, and why might resizing it to fit the average day fail to solve the Monday problem?
lessons.teach:
Scaling a database instance means changing the resources of the server that runs the database. The main resources are CPU (processing power), memory (RAM, which holds frequently used data so it does not have to be read from disk), storage (disk space), and I/O capacity (how quickly the disk can read and write). Making the machine bigger in these ways is called vertical scaling. Adding more machines to share the load is horizontal scaling, which is a different decision handled elsewhere in this unit.

Why it works: a database slows down when one resource runs out. When CPU stays near full, queries queue up. When memory is too small, reads that could come from RAM go to disk instead. When storage fills, writes fail. So you watch utilization, decide what the workload needs, and resize before the limit is reached.

Worked example: an orders database averages 55 percent CPU over a normal week, but peaks at 90 percent around lunchtime. Step one: record the peak, not just the average. Step two: choose a target peak utilization, say 70 percent, to leave headroom for surprises. Step three: estimate the change. 90 divided by 70 is about 1.3, so CPU capacity should grow by roughly 30 percent, which likely means moving up one machine size. Step four: schedule the change before the next known sales event.

Storage is a special case. Many managed services can grow storage automatically, but they often cannot shrink it again, so growing storage too far is a lasting cost.

Common mistake: sizing to average load instead of peak load. The database looks fine on paper and then fails at the busiest hour.

Consequence: a resize that requires a restart causes a short outage, so connections drop and applications see errors during that window. Planned changes belong in a maintenance window with a rollback plan, and the size chosen should keep peak utilization below the target you set.

questions.prompt: A clinic booking database runs on a managed service. Its working set, meaning the data it needs in memory at the same time, reaches 22 GB at the Monday 9 a.m. peak. The team wants peak memory use to stay at or below 75 percent of total RAM. The sizing notes so far: Step 1, record the peak working set: 22 GB. Step 2, set the target: the peak must fit within 75 percent of RAM. Step 3 is missing from the notes. Step 4, choose a machine size and schedule the change in a maintenance window, is still to come. Which step 3 completes the sizing?
choices: Use the weekly average working set of 9 GB as the memory target, since averages describe normal use.
Divide 22 GB by 0.75 to get about 29.3 GB of total RAM needed, then round up to a size of at least 30 GB.
Multiply 22 GB by 0.75 to get 16.5 GB, then buy a machine with 16.5 GB of RAM.
Add 25 percent to the disk size, because memory and disk always need to grow by the same amount.
questions.why: The target says the peak must be no more than 75 percent of total RAM, so total RAM must be the peak divided by 0.75, rounded up to an available size.

questions.prompt: Which resource does a database use to keep frequently read data close at hand so it does not have to be fetched from disk every time?
choices: I/O capacity, because it sets how fast writes reach the disk.
Memory (RAM), because it holds frequently used data for fast reads.
CPU, because it runs the queries that request the data.
Storage, because it holds the full set of tables on disk.
questions.why: The teaching text defines memory as the resource that holds frequently used data so reads can avoid going to disk.

questions.prompt: A team on a managed database service grew storage from 500 GB to 2 TB to get through a temporary spike in data volume. The spike is now over and the data is back to normal size. What is the most likely lasting consequence of that choice?
choices: The service will automatically shrink the storage back to 500 GB within a day.
The larger storage size likely stays in place and keeps costing money, because such services often cannot shrink storage.
The database will run slower because the disk is larger than it needs to be.
Writes will start failing once the normal data volume is reached again.
questions.why: The teaching text notes that storage can often grow automatically but often cannot shrink, so growing it too far is a lasting cost.

questions.prompt: A reporting database averages 40 percent CPU across the month but reaches 95 percent CPU on the last day of each month. The team's target peak utilization is 70 percent. Roughly how much more CPU capacity does the instance need to stay within the target at month end?
choices: About 57 percent more, because 40 divided by 70 is about 0.57.
About 5 percent more, based on the gap between the peak and the target.
About 36 percent more, because 95 divided by 70 is about 1.36.
No increase, because the 40 percent average is below the target.
questions.why: Peak divided by target gives the growth factor, 95 divided by 70 is about 1.36, so CPU capacity should rise by roughly 36 percent; the average is the wrong basis for sizing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would size a database instance ahead of a known sales event next month. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the current numbers: look at CPU, memory, storage and disk I/O over several normal weeks, and focus on the peaks rather than the averages. Then I would compare the expected sales-event load against those peaks, using the known traffic growth, and pick a size that keeps peak utilization around 70 percent so there is room for surprises. I would schedule the resize before the event, in a maintenance window, because a resize that requires a restart will drop connections for a short time. The tradeoff is cost: a larger instance stays expensive after the event unless we plan to scale back down, and scaling down needs its own planned window and a check that the smaller size still handles normal peaks. Storage is different because it can usually grow but often cannot shrink, so I would grow it conservatively.
rubricPoints: Sizing is based on peak utilization, not the average, against a target headroom.
Resources such as CPU, memory, storage and I/O each need checking, not just one.
Resizing may require a restart, so it should be scheduled in a maintenance window.
Scaling up is a cost tradeoff, and storage often cannot be shrunk once grown.

suggested.rationale: Autoscaling policies let a learner reason about current and upcoming load against capacity thresholds, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Replication means keeping more than one copy of the same data, on more than one machine, and keeping those copies up to date. One copy takes the writes and is called the primary. The others follow it and are called replicas. If the main machine breaks, a copy can take over, and readers can be spread across copies to take load off the primary. The hard part is timing. A copy may trail behind the primary for a moment, and how you set that trade-off decides what you can lose and what a reader might see. Think of a newspaper printing the same edition on several presses fed from one master plate. Each press runs a little behind the master, and one jammed press does not stop the others.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database has a primary and one replica in another building. A customer changes their delivery address. The primary accepts the change and confirms it, then the primary's machine fails a moment later, before the replica has received the change. The replica is promoted to become the new primary. What does the customer see afterwards, and why?
lessons.teach:
A replica is a copy of a database that receives changes from the primary, the instance that accepts writes. Replication is the process of shipping those changes from the primary to its replicas. Two timing strategies matter. In synchronous replication, the primary does not confirm a write to the client until at least one standby has also stored it. In asynchronous replication, the primary confirms the write as soon as it is stored locally, and sends the change to replicas afterwards. Synchronous replication loses nothing when a failure happens, but every write waits for the round trip to the standby, so it is slower and can stall when the link is slow. Asynchronous replication is faster but leaves a gap. The distance between what the primary has applied and what a replica has applied is called replication lag. Any change still inside that gap is lost if the primary fails and the replica is promoted.

Why this works: a replica applies changes in the same order the primary produced them, so at any moment it is a consistent but possibly older picture of the data.

Worked example. At 09:00:00 the primary commits a seat assignment and confirms it to the app. The replica is two seconds behind, so it has not applied that change yet. Step one, the commit lands on the primary. Step two, the confirmation goes back to the app. Step three, the change is shipped to the replica. Step four, the replica applies it. If a read goes to the replica at 09:00:01, it returns the old seat. If the primary fails at 09:00:01 and the replica is promoted, the assignment is gone. The window between step two and step four is the exposure.

Common mistake: treating a replica as a backup. Replication copies a bad DELETE or a corrupted write as faithfully as a good one, so it protects against machine failure, not against human error.

Consequence in a running system: a dashboard that reads from a lagging replica shows stale positions. Lag that grows without anyone noticing is the first sign that the replica cannot keep up with write volume.

questions.prompt: Harborline Tickets keeps its order database on a primary that accepts writes. It has one synchronous standby, meaning a copy kept ready to take over that must store each write before the primary can confirm it, and one asynchronous reporting replica, which receives changes after the primary has already confirmed them. At 14:10:00 the order service commits a 40 dollar refund on the primary. Step one: the refund is stored on the primary. Step two: the synchronous standby stores the same refund and reports back to the primary. Step three: [missing]. Step four: the reporting replica receives the refund and applies it. What belongs in step three?
choices: The primary confirms the refund to the order service, because the synchronous standby already holds it.
The primary waits for the reporting replica to apply the refund before it confirms anything.
The reporting replica confirms the refund to the order service before it applies anything.
The standby sends the refund back to the primary so it is committed a second time.
questions.why: Under synchronous replication the primary confirms a write once at least one synchronous standby has stored it, and the asynchronous reporting replica does not gate that confirmation.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Logistics runs a primary with one asynchronous replica. Monitoring shows the replica's replication lag at 45 seconds at noon and 3 minutes at 18:00, while write volume has risen steadily. What is the best reading of this trend?
choices: The primary has a hardware fault and should be replaced immediately.
The replica cannot keep up with write volume, and the growing gap is the early warning sign.
Asynchronous replication is removing changes from the replica on purpose.
The replica is correct and the lag figure is a display error.
questions.why: Replication lag that grows over time means the replica is applying changes more slowly than the primary produces them, which is the warning sign described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A payments team uses asynchronous replication to a standby in another location. At the moment the primary fails, the replica is 3 seconds behind. The team promotes the standby to primary. Which statement is true?
choices: Only the writes committed in the last 3 seconds before failure, which the standby had not applied, may be missing.
The primary's writes from the last 3 seconds are automatically replayed from the failed machine.
The whole database is lost, because the standby holds no data at all.
Nothing is lost, because asynchronous replication always waits for the standby.
questions.why: Changes inside the replication lag gap were confirmed by the failed primary but not yet applied on the standby, so they are lost when that standby is promoted.

questions.prompt: A team says their replica is their backup because every write reaches it. A developer then runs a DELETE on the primary that removes the wrong customer rows. What is the main weakness in the team's reasoning?
choices: Replication copies the bad DELETE as faithfully as a good write, so the replica loses the same rows.
Replicas are slower to restore than backups, so the team should have waited.
Replicas only copy inserts, so the DELETE never reached them.
The primary blocks deletes from being replicated to protect the replicas.
questions.why: Replication protects against machine failure but not against human error, because a harmful change is shipped to the replica just like a correct one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication for a read-heavy service. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Synchronous replication means the primary waits until a standby has stored the write before it confirms to the client. Nothing confirmed is lost if the primary fails, but every write pays the round trip to the standby, so write latency rises and the primary can stall if the link is slow. Asynchronous replication confirms as soon as the primary stores the write and ships the change afterwards. Writes are fast, but the gap between primary and replica, the replication lag, is exposed. Changes inside that gap are lost on failover, and reads from a replica can return older data. For a read-heavy service I would put asynchronous read replicas in front of the reads, because they scale reads cheaply. The tradeoff I would state plainly is that readers can see data that is seconds old, so anything that must read its own writes should go to the primary or check the lag first.
rubricPoints: Defines synchronous replication as waiting for a standby before confirming the write
Defines asynchronous replication as confirming first and shipping later, with replication lag as the gap
Names a concrete cost: added write latency for synchronous, possible data loss or stale reads for asynchronous
Gives a sensible choice for the stated workload and the limit that comes with it

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner diagnose stale reads from a lagging replica, which is the main consequence of asynchronous replication taught here.

lessons.plain: Cost work on a database means knowing what the setup costs you each month and making it cheaper without making it unreliable. A database bill is made of several pieces: the machine that runs it, the disk space it reserves, the input and output work it does, the backups it keeps, and the extra copies it runs for safety. Assessing cost means measuring which of these you actually use. Optimizing means adjusting them, such as shrinking an oversized machine or deleting old backups nobody needs. It is continuous because workloads change over time, so a setup that was right last year may be wasteful now.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database runs on a machine sized for its busiest day, but on most days that machine is only about 15 percent busy. What do you think happens to the monthly bill if you keep paying for that big machine all month, and what would you check before making it smaller?
lessons.teach:
Cost assessment means finding out what each part of a database solution costs and whether you are paying for capacity you do not use. A database bill usually has a few main parts. Compute is the processing capacity, measured in virtual CPUs (the processing units) and memory (RAM, the fast working space). Storage is the disk space you provision, which you pay for whether or not it is full. Input and output (I/O) is the read and write work the disk does, which some services charge for separately. Backups and retained history consume storage too. Replicas, which are extra copies that serve reads or stand by in case of failure, each cost roughly as much as the database they copy. Network traffic leaving a region can also cost money.

Why this works: cost follows provisioned size, not actual use, so measured idle margin is money you can recover. The method is to watch utilization over a representative period that includes the busiest day, then compare peak use with what is provisioned. If peak CPU stays under about half for weeks, the machine may be one size too large. You then change the size in a planned window and watch the vitals again to confirm reliability has not dropped.

Worked example: a reporting database has 16 vCPU and 64 GB of RAM. Over 30 days, CPU peaks at 22 percent and memory at 38 percent. Step 1: note the provisioned size and its monthly cost. Step 2: record peak use, not the average, so a monthly batch job is not missed. Step 3: choose a smaller size with headroom, perhaps 4 vCPU and 16 GB. Step 4: schedule the change off-peak, then recheck utilization for two weeks.

Common mistake: sizing down based on average CPU, which hides a short peak. In a running system, the cheaper machine may slow to a crawl during the batch window and miss a reporting deadline, so every cost cut must be verified against the same real workload.

Cost optimization is a repeated measurement cycle, not a one-time check of the price list.

questions.prompt: A small online ticketing company runs one managed relational database (a database service that Google runs the server software for) with 4 TB of provisioned SSD storage (solid-state disk, a fast flash drive) at a fixed monthly price per TB. Actual data is 900 GB and grows about 40 GB per month. The team wants to shrink the disk to save money, and works through these steps. Step 1: note the provisioned size and its monthly storage cost. Step 2: record the peak data size and the growth rate over the last 90 days, not the average. Step 3: this step is missing from the notes. Step 4: schedule the resize in a planned window, then check disk usage again over the next two weeks. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: Pick a target disk size that covers the peak data plus projected growth over the planning period, with a safety margin.
Move the data to a faster disk type, because a faster disk always costs less per GB than a slower one.
Multiply the number of read replicas (extra copies that serve reads) by the disk size to find the total bill.
Delete older backups first, because backup retention (how long old backups are kept) is the largest storage cost.
questions.why: The missing step is choosing a new size that still fits the real peak and expected growth with margin, which is what keeps the cheaper disk from filling up after the resize.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a read replica, and why does it affect a cost review?
choices: A second network connection that only costs money when it sends data out of the region.
A free copy the provider makes automatically, so it adds no cost to the bill.
An extra copy of a database that serves reads or stands by for failure, and each one costs roughly as much as the database it copies.
A backup file kept for recovery, which is charged only for the network traffic it generates.
questions.why: A read replica is an extra running copy of the database, so each one adds a cost close to the original, which makes replicas a common target in a cost review.

questions.prompt: A team runs a database with 12 vCPU (virtual CPUs, the processing units). Over 60 days, the peak CPU was 41 percent, and that peak came during month-end close. Someone proposes cutting to 2 vCPU because the average CPU is only about 12 percent. Which approach best follows a sound cost review?
choices: Cut to 8 vCPU, judged against the 60-day peak including month-end, then recheck utilization after the change.
Cut to 6 vCPU, because half of the current size is always enough headroom.
Cut to 2 vCPU now, because the average CPU shows the machine is mostly idle.
Keep 12 vCPU, because any reduction in processing capacity risks an outage.
questions.why: Sizing from the peak, which here includes month-end, and then verifying after the change is the method that protects reliability while still recovering idle margin.

questions.prompt: A team cut their database from a larger size to a smaller one after measuring CPU over only the most recent 7 days, which were quiet. At quarter-end, the heavy reporting run missed its deadline. Which statement identifies the real flaw in their cost review?
choices: They should have removed the replicas first, since replicas always cost more than the primary database.
They measured over a window that missed the busiest period, and they did not verify the smaller size against the real heavy workload afterward.
They should have billed storage per GB rather than per vCPU, since storage is the largest line on the bill.
They should have measured memory instead of CPU, since memory is always the limit for reporting jobs.
questions.why: A cost cut must be measured over a representative period that includes the peak, and then confirmed against the same real workload, which this team did not do.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find and reduce unnecessary database spend on a running system, and name one limit or risk of cutting costs.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing what the database bills for: machine size, provisioned storage, replicas, backups, and network egress. Then I would look at utilization over a full cycle, including the busiest period, rather than averages, because sizing down to fit an average can break a peak job. Typical candidates are machines with low peak use, storage provisioned far above what is stored, backups kept beyond the retention we need, and replicas nobody reads from.
