I would change one thing at a time in a planned window and watch latency, errors, and replica lag afterward. The main limit is reliability: a smaller instance has less headroom, so a saving that pushes peak CPU near its ceiling is a false saving. Removing a replica or shortening backup retention also weakens recovery, so each saving has to be weighed against the recovery target the business needs.
rubricPoints: Names the main cost parts: compute, provisioned storage, I/O, backups, replicas, and network egress.
Uses peak utilization over a full cycle, not averages, to decide on right-sizing.
Changes one thing at a time and verifies reliability afterward.
States the tradeoff: less headroom or fewer copies can hurt reliability or recovery.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits lets the learner compare sizing and replica choices and see the reliability tradeoff without spending real money.

lessons.plain: Optimizing a query means changing how a database finds the rows you asked for so it does less work. A query is a question you send to a database, such as 'give me the orders for this customer.' If the database has to read every row to answer it, that costs time, computing power and, on many cloud services, money, because you are often billed for the data read. Good optimization means the database reads only what it needs. You check this by looking at how it actually ran the question rather than guessing. Speed and cost usually improve together, so engineers treat them as one job.
lessons.guessPrompt: A table has 10 million orders and you ask for the orders of one customer. Without any special help, roughly how much of the table do you think the database must read, and what single change would most reduce that?
lessons.teach:
A query plan is the strategy a database picks to answer a question: which tables to read, in what order, and whether it uses a shortcut. A full table scan reads every row and checks each one. An index is a separate, sorted structure built on one or more columns, much like the alphabetical index at the back of a book, that lets the database jump straight to matching rows. Selectivity describes how few rows a filter keeps. A filter that keeps 12 of 10 million rows is highly selective, and an index pays off most for filters like that. Partitioning splits a large table into pieces by a column such as date, so a query that filters on that column can skip whole pieces. This is called partition pruning.

Why it works: the cost of a query tracks the amount of data it touches. Reading fewer rows means less CPU, less disk input and output, and, in services that bill by bytes scanned, a smaller bill.

Worked example: SELECT order_id, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42, on a 10 million row table. Step 1: with no index, the database reads all 10 million rows and tests customer_id on each one. Step 2: after you create an index on customer_id, the database looks up 42 in the sorted index, finds the 12 matching row locations, and reads only those. Step 3: you confirm with the plan output that it shows an index lookup rather than a scan. Selecting only the two needed columns, instead of every column, reduces the data read further.

Common mistake: wrapping the indexed column in a function, such as WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2024-05-01'. This stops the index being used, because the stored values no longer match the search. Compare the raw column against a range instead.

Consequence: in a running system, one unindexed query repeated by a busy API can saturate disk and CPU, slow every other request sharing the instance, and push the monthly bill up. Measure the plan first, change the query or index second, and measure again.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps 40 million parcel scan events in a table called scan_events. The table is partitioned by scan_date, with one partition per day across three years, so a query that filters on scan_date can skip the partitions it does not need. A dashboard runs: SELECT parcel_id, hub_code FROM scan_events WHERE scan_date = '2024-03-15' AND hub_code = 'LDN-4'. Step 1: the filter on scan_date lets the database skip every daily partition except 2024-03-15, so it reads about 110,000 rows instead of 40 million. Step 2: the database tests hub_code on those 110,000 rows and keeps the matches. Step 3, which is the one left for you: the team wants to confirm that the query is using the partition skip and not reading everything. What should they do?
choices: Add every column to the SELECT list so the plan output shows more detail
Check the plan output and confirm it shows the partition pruning rather than a full scan of all partitions
Remove the scan_date filter so the planner can choose the cheapest plan on its own
Wrap scan_date in a function such as DATE(scan_date) so the planner has a second filter to work with
questions.why: The plan output shows whether the database skipped partitions, which is the confirmation step the teaching text describes after a change.

questions.prompt: A clickstream table holds 500 million rows. A filter on one column keeps only about 2,000 of them. Which description fits that filter?
choices: Low selectivity, because the filter keeps most of the rows and an index would rarely help
High selectivity, because the table has a large number of columns
High selectivity, because the filter keeps a very small share of the rows, which is where an index pays off most
Selectivity measures how quickly the disk can write new rows to the table
questions.why: Selectivity describes how few rows a filter keeps, and a filter keeping 2,000 of 500 million rows is highly selective.

questions.prompt: A reporting query runs against a 200-million-row sales table that is partitioned by sale_date. The query filters sale_date to a single week. What can the database do for this query?
choices: Copy the whole table into a new table before answering the query
Read every partition, because partitioning only speeds up inserts and never reads
Skip every partition outside that week, which is partition pruning
Ignore the date filter and fall back to a full scan of every row
questions.why: Partitioning splits the table by date so a filter on that date lets the database skip the partitions outside the week.

questions.prompt: A support tool runs WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com' against a 60-million-row tickets table. There is an index on the email column, but the query plan shows a full scan. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The equality check always forces a full scan regardless of any index
LOWER() adds more columns to the result, which forces the planner to read every row
Wrapping the column in LOWER() means the stored values no longer match the search, so the index cannot be used
Indexes cannot be built on text columns, so the planner always scans
questions.why: Applying a function to the indexed column changes the values being compared, so the sorted index no longer lines up with the search and the planner falls back to a scan.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a query can be fast in a test database and slow in production, and name one tradeoff of adding an index.
lessons.modelAnswer: A test database usually holds a few thousand rows, so even a full scan finishes quickly and nobody notices the missing index. Production holds millions of rows, so the same query reads far more data, uses more CPU and disk, and may compete with other requests. The fix is usually to check the query plan on realistic data volume and add an index on the filtered columns. The tradeoff is that every index takes storage and must be updated on each insert, update and delete, so writes get slower and cost more. So before adding one, I check that the query runs often enough and filters selectively enough to justify it, and I remove indexes that nothing uses.
rubricPoints: Explains that test data volume hides the cost of full scans that production exposes
Describes checking the query plan on realistic data before and after a change
Names the tradeoff that indexes add storage cost and slow writes
Notes that an index is justified only for frequent, selective queries

suggested.rationale: The planned SQL lab would let the learner run the same query before and after an index and read the plan, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Database maintenance is the routine upkeep that keeps a database fast and recoverable after it has been running for a while. Two common tasks are rebuilding indexes and making copies of data with exports. An index is a sorted lookup structure that lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, a bit like the index at the back of a book. As rows are added, changed and deleted, indexes can become bloated and out of order, so queries slow down. Rebuilding an index writes it out again compactly. An export copies data out in a portable form, which is useful for archives, moving data, or checking what is stored. Both tasks use resources and need planning.
lessons.guessPrompt: A query on a large orders table has become slower over the past year, even though the data has grown only gradually. Name one maintenance task you would check first and say why, before you know anything else about the database.
lessons.teach:
Start with the terms. A table is a set of rows. An index is a separate structure kept alongside a table that stores one or more columns' values in sorted order, with pointers back to the matching rows, so a lookup can jump to the matches instead of scanning every row. Fragmentation means that after many inserts, updates and deletes, the index's storage pages are partly empty or sit out of physical order. Statistics are the database's summaries of how many rows exist and how values are spread across them; the query planner uses them to decide between using an index and scanning the table. A logical export writes rows and table definitions out as portable files or statements, as opposed to copying the raw storage files.

Why it works: a rebuild writes the index again from the current rows, packing pages tightly and in order, so a read touches fewer pages. Refreshing statistics afterwards lets the planner see the real shape of the data and pick a sensible plan.

Worked example: an orders table has an index on customer_id. After a year of deletes, the index pages are roughly half empty. Step 1: read the fragmentation or page-density figure the engine reports for that index. Step 2: schedule a rebuild in a quiet window. Step 3: the engine builds a fresh copy of the index from the table rows. Step 4: refresh the statistics for the table. Step 5: rerun the slow query and compare how many pages it reads before and after.

Common mistake: rebuilding every index on a fixed timer without measuring first. A rebuild uses CPU and disk I/O, can block writes while it runs, and gains little on an index that is already compact. Similarly, an export taken during heavy writes may not be a consistent picture unless the tool reads from a fixed point in time.

On a live service, a rebuild that locks a busy table can stall writes and cause timeouts across the whole application, so it belongs in a maintenance window with a rollback plan and a fresh export taken beforehand.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps a sensor_readings table with an index on device_id. After a year of purges the engine reports that the index pages are only 41 percent full. Here is the maintenance plan. Step 1: read the page-density figure for the device_id index, which is 41 percent. Step 2: this step is missing and you must fill it. Step 3: schedule the rebuild for the 02:00 to 03:00 window. Step 4: refresh the statistics on sensor_readings. Which action belongs in the missing Step 2, before the rebuild?
choices: Rebuild every index on every table in the database on a fixed weekly timer
Take a logical export of sensor_readings that reads from a fixed point in time, so there is a rollback copy
Turn off the query planner so it stops relying on statistics
Delete all readings older than 90 days to shrink the table
questions.why: A rebuild can block writes and may go wrong, so a consistent export taken from a fixed point in time before the work starts is the safety net, and it must come before the rebuild rather than after.

questions.prompt: On a billing database, an index on invoice_date reports that its pages are about 95 percent full and stored in near-sorted order. What is the most sensible next step?
choices: Rebuild it, then turn off statistics so the planner uses the index
Leave it alone and measure again later, because a rebuild would cost I/O and gain little
Drop the table and reload it from scratch
Rebuild it now, since any index older than a month needs one
questions.why: An index that is already compact and in order gains little from a rebuild, while the rebuild still consumes CPU and disk I/O, so measuring first is the right move.

questions.prompt: A nightly logical export of a shipping-manifest table starts at 23:00 and runs for 90 minutes, while the application keeps writing rows the whole time. What is the main risk to the export?
choices: The export will automatically rebuild the index on the destination system
The export cannot be restored into a different project or region
The export may not be a consistent picture, because rows written during the 90 minutes can land in some parts of the output and not others, unless the tool reads from a fixed point in time
The export will be smaller than the table because indexes are excluded from it
questions.why: Without a fixed point in time, a long export during heavy writes can capture some rows before a change and others after it, so it does not represent one moment.

questions.prompt: What does a logical export of a database table produce?
choices: A summary of how many rows each value appears in, used by the planner
A byte-for-byte copy of the disk files that hold the table
A new index built from the current rows
Rows and table definitions written out as portable files or statements
questions.why: A logical export writes rows and table definitions as portable files or statements, which is different from copying the raw storage files, the statistics summaries, or an index.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would rebuild an index and when you would leave it alone, and name one risk of running a rebuild or an export against a busy production database.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would rebuild an index only after measuring that it is actually fragmented or bloated and that a slow query is reading far more pages than the rows it returns. If the index is already compact, or the table is mostly reads on a stable dataset, a rebuild just burns CPU and disk for no gain. After a rebuild I would refresh the table statistics so the planner uses the new layout. The main risk on a busy production database is locking or heavy I/O: a rebuild can block writes on the table or slow every other query, so I would run it in a low-traffic window with a current export as a fallback. An export carries a similar risk, since it adds read load and may not be consistent if writes are happening during the copy.
rubricPoints: A rebuild should be triggered by measured fragmentation or slow queries, not by a fixed timer alone.
A rebuild rewrites the index compactly from current rows and should be followed by refreshing statistics.
A rebuild or export can add CPU, I/O, and locking pressure on a live database, so timing matters.
An export is a portable logical copy, and its consistency depends on reading from a fixed point in time.

suggested.rationale: Deciding when to rebuild an index and checking its effect on a query plan is best practised by running SQL against a database, which the planned SQL lab would provide.

lessons.plain: A database export is a copy of the data written out as a file, such as a SQL dump, that you can keep somewhere else and load back later. Scheduling exports means setting things up so the copy is made automatically on a fixed rhythm, like every night at 2 a.m., without someone remembering to press a button. Think of it like photocopying a ledger at the same time each night and filing the copy in a cabinet. The schedule decides how old your newest copy can be when something goes wrong. The file location and how long you keep old copies decide whether those copies still exist when you need them. Good scheduling means choosing the time, checking that each run finished, and deleting old copies on purpose.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your orders database gets a fresh export every night at 02:00 and you keep the last 30 files. If the database fails at noon, roughly how much recent data could be missing from the newest file you can restore?
lessons.teach:
An export is a job that reads a database and writes its contents to a file outside the live database, usually as a logical dump of SQL statements or as CSV rows. A storage bucket is a container for files in cloud object storage. A scheduler is a service that starts a job at times you set, using a cron expression, which is a compact timetable: 0 2 * * * means 02:00 every day. Retention is how long copies are kept before deletion. A lifecycle rule is a bucket setting that deletes files once they reach a set age.

Why it works: the export runs on the schedule, so nobody has to remember it. The scheduler calls the database's export operation with a destination path, and the database service does the reading and writes the file. Each run produces a new file, often named with a date, so older copies are not overwritten.

Worked example: the scheduler fires at 02:00 UTC. Step 1: it calls the export operation for the orders database. Step 2: the database writes orders-2024-06-10.sql into a bucket. Step 3: the job reports success or failure. Step 4: a lifecycle rule deletes files older than 30 days. Result: there are about 30 daily copies at any time, and the newest is at most about 24 hours old, so the recovery point is roughly one day.

Common mistake: treating an export as a backup you can roll back to at any minute. An export is a snapshot from the moment it ran, and restoring it is slower than restoring an automated backup. Another mistake is never checking job status, so failures go unnoticed for weeks.

Consequence: an export reads the whole database, which uses CPU and disk I/O on the running instance. Scheduling it at peak traffic can slow user queries, so run it in a quiet window and watch latency while it runs. Scheduling an export is only worthwhile when you can see each run succeed and know how old the newest copy is.

questions.prompt: Harbor Tickets keeps a support-ticket database. Its scheduler uses the cron expression 0 */6 * * *, which is a compact timetable meaning minute 0 of every sixth hour, so runs start at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00 UTC. The team traces one run, and Step 2 has been left blank. Step 1: the scheduler fires at 06:00 UTC and calls the export operation for the tickets database with a destination path. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the job reports success or failure. Step 4: a lifecycle rule deletes files older than 7 days. Which choice correctly completes the missing Step 2?
choices: The database service reads the tickets and writes a new file with a dated name into the bucket, so earlier copies are not overwritten.
The scheduler reads every ticket row itself and writes the file into the bucket.
The lifecycle rule writes the new file and then deletes the oldest copy in the same step.
The export operation overwrites the previous file with the same name, so only one copy ever exists.
questions.why: The database service does the reading and writes a new, dated file, which is why each run leaves earlier copies in place; the other choices give the reading or writing job to the wrong component or describe overwriting, which the teaching text says does not happen.

questions.prompt: A teammate reads the cron expression 30 22 * * * and asks what it means. Which answer is correct?
choices: At 22:30 every day.
Every 22 minutes, starting at half past the hour.
Every 30 seconds during the 22nd hour of each month.
At 22:30 on the 30th day of every month.
questions.why: In a cron expression the fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, so 30 22 with stars elsewhere means 22:30 every day.

questions.prompt: A team exports its orders database every night to a bucket with a 30-day lifecycle rule, but nobody looks at the job status. The export has been failing for three weeks. What is the most accurate description of the risk?
choices: The database will be locked from reads until someone checks the job status.
The newest good copy keeps getting older while the team assumes it is about a day old, so the recovery point has drifted back and nobody knows.
The scheduler will automatically retry each failed export until one succeeds.
The lifecycle rule will stop deleting files, so the bucket will grow without limit.
questions.why: Failures that go unnoticed mean the newest successful file keeps aging while the team believes it is recent, which is the failure case the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A team plans to export a busy customer database at 14:00 UTC, which is its peak traffic time. What should the engineer do before or while the export runs?
choices: Schedule it at 14:00 anyway, since the export only reads and cannot affect user queries.
Delete the lifecycle rule so the export does not compete with cleanup jobs.
Move the export to a quiet window and watch query latency while the export runs.
Turn off the scheduler and run the export by hand whenever a user complains.
questions.why: An export reads the whole database and uses CPU and disk I/O on the running instance, so it should run in a quiet window with latency watched during the run.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a scheduled database export gives you, what it does not give you, and one tradeoff in choosing when it runs.
lessons.modelAnswer: A scheduled export gives us a regular file copy of the database, made without anyone having to remember it, and stored outside the live system. The copy is only as fresh as the last successful run. If we export nightly, the newest file can be up to about a day old, so that is the most data we could lose on a restore. It does not give us point-in-time recovery, which means rolling back to any chosen minute. Restoring from an export is also slower than restoring an automated backup, because the whole file has to be loaded back. The main tradeoff is timing. Exports read the whole database, so running them at peak hours can slow live queries and consume I/O. Running them in a quiet window lowers that impact but makes the recovery point older. We should also confirm each run's status and set retention so old files are deleted on purpose.
rubricPoints: An export is a file copy that is only as recent as its last successful run
Exports are not point-in-time recovery and restore more slowly than automated backups
Scheduled exports load the running database, so timing affects live performance
Each run must be checked for success, and retention determines how many copies exist

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly configuration facts and scheduling choices with no existing or planned OpsForge hands-on engine that practices export scheduling directly.

lessons.plain: A managed database is one where the cloud provider runs the database software for you. Upgrading it means moving that software to a newer version to get security fixes, bug fixes, and new features, while the provider handles much of the mechanics. The hard part is not the button press. It is choosing when the upgrade happens, because an upgrade can briefly interrupt connections, can change how queries behave, and may not be reversible by simply going back. Think of renovating a shop that stays open: you pick the quiet hour, test the new layout first, and keep a plan ready in case customers start complaining.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your managed database has a new minor version available and a maintenance window every Sunday at 02:00. Before reading on, what would you check before letting the upgrade run, and what would you do if the application broke afterwards?
lessons.teach:
A minor version upgrade changes the database engine to a newer release within the same major line, usually carrying fixes and patches. A major version upgrade moves to a new major line, which can change behaviour, deprecate features, and alter how queries are planned. A maintenance window is a recurring time slot you choose in which the provider may apply updates, and it usually causes a short restart, so connections drop briefly. Some services allow you to defer an update for a limited period, which buys time but does not remove the need to upgrade. A point-in-time recovery backup lets you restore the database to a moment just before the upgrade.

Worked example, for a managed PostgreSQL instance moving from major version 14 to 15. Step 1: read the release notes and note any behaviour changes that touch your queries. Step 2: clone the production instance into a staging copy. Step 3: upgrade the clone and run your real application test suite and a sample of production queries, timing them. Step 4: take an on-demand backup of production, then schedule the upgrade inside the agreed window. Step 5: after the upgrade, check error rates, latency, and connection counts for an hour, and keep the backup until you are confident.

Common mistake: trusting that a maintenance window is safe without testing, or upgrading immediately before any backup. A major upgrade generally cannot be reversed in place, so the rollback path is restoring a backup into a new instance, which takes time and means losing writes made after the backup unless you recover to a point in time.

In a running system, a skipped test can turn a quiet Sunday into a Monday outage. The safe habit is to rehearse the upgrade on a clone and know your restore time before you touch production.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a managed PostgreSQL 15 instance that stores shipment records. The provider has published a minor-version patch and offers a 14-day deferral. The team first read the patch notes, which list only security and crash fixes and no behaviour changes. They then chose to use the deferral to push the patch back while they finish a software release. When the release slipped, they looked at the calendar with one day left on the deferral. The step they have not yet taken is to schedule the patch into a maintenance window before the deferral ends, since deferral only buys time.
choices: Upgrade the instance to the next major version so the pending minor patch is no longer needed
Take a point-in-time backup of the instance and then leave the patch pending until the next release
Ask the provider to extend the deferral indefinitely so the patch never has to be applied
Schedule the patch into a maintenance window before the deferral runs out, because deferral buys time but does not remove the need to upgrade
questions.why: A deferral only postpones the update for a limited period, so the team must still apply it inside a maintenance window before the deferral expires.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a minor and a major version upgrade of a managed database?
choices: A minor upgrade moves to a new major line, while a major upgrade only carries bug fixes
Both kinds of upgrade are identical in risk, and the only difference is the length of the maintenance window
A minor upgrade always requires a new instance, while a major upgrade is applied in place
A minor upgrade stays within the same major release line and usually carries fixes, while a major upgrade moves to a new major line that can change behaviour and query planning
questions.why: A minor upgrade stays on the same major line and mostly brings fixes, while a major upgrade moves to a new major line that can change behaviour, deprecate features, and alter query plans.

questions.prompt: A payments startup runs a managed MySQL instance with a Saturday 01:00 to 02:00 maintenance window. During that window the provider applies an update that causes a short restart. What should the application do so customers see the least disruption?
choices: Keep every connection open and let the database hold them through the restart
Stop accepting payments for the whole day so no connection is attempted during the window
Retry dropped connections with a short back-off so brief restarts do not surface as failed payments
Move all traffic to a new database instance before the window and leave it there permanently
questions.why: A maintenance restart drops connections briefly, so the application should reconnect with a back-off instead of failing or assuming connections survive.

questions.prompt: A retail team upgraded its managed database to a new major version directly in production, right after a nightly backup taken at 23:00. The next morning a serious application bug appears and the team wants to return to the old version. Which rollback approach matches how a major upgrade is usually reversed?
choices: Wait for the provider to roll back the upgrade automatically after the bug is reported
Replay the application logs against the new version until the bug disappears
Restore the 23:00 backup into a new instance, accepting that writes made after 23:00 are lost unless they recover to a point just before the upgrade
Downgrade the same instance in place with a single console command, with no data loss
questions.why: A major upgrade generally cannot be reversed in place, so rollback means restoring a backup into a new instance, and writes after the backup are lost unless a point-in-time recovery is used.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate suggests we turn on automatic upgrades for our managed database and never think about upgrades again. Explain to them, in your own words, what automatic or scheduled upgrades do and do not protect you from, and name one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Scheduled upgrades mean the provider applies updates during a window we choose, which removes the manual work and keeps us on supported, patched software. But they do not check that our application still works. A minor update usually has a small behaviour risk, and a major version change can alter query plans, deprecate features, or break a driver. The upgrade also causes a short restart, so applications without retry logic will show errors during it. Once a major version is applied, it generally cannot be rolled back in place, so our real protection is a recent backup, a tested restore time, and a staging copy we upgrade first. Automatic upgrades are fine for patches, but we should still test before major changes.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes minor from major version upgrades and their different risks
Explains that scheduled upgrades cause brief downtime or dropped connections
Notes that a major upgrade usually cannot be reverted in place
Recommends testing on a staging clone and taking a backup before the upgrade

suggested.rationale: No listed mission covers managed database upgrades, so an exam-style scenario asking the learner to choose an upgrade path and rollback plan adds the most.

lessons.plain: An SLA, or service level agreement, is a promise a provider makes to a customer, often with money or service credits at stake if it is broken. An SLO, or service level objective, is the internal target a team sets so it keeps that promise, such as keeping database queries fast for 99.9 percent of the month. An SLI, or service level indicator, is the measurement behind the target, like the fraction of requests that succeeded. Monitoring these means choosing the few numbers that reflect what users actually feel, measuring them continuously, and warning people before a target is missed rather than after.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a database must be available 99.9 percent of a 30-day month, roughly how many minutes of downtime does that allow, and what would you think if 35 of those minutes were already used by day 10?
lessons.teach: Start with three terms. A service level indicator (SLI) is a measurement of how the service behaves from the user's side, written as a ratio of good events to total events. For a database this might be the share of queries that return within 200 milliseconds, or the share of connection attempts that succeed. A service level objective (SLO) is the target you set for that measurement over a window, for example 99.9 percent of queries under 200 milliseconds across a rolling 30 days. A service level agreement (SLA) is the external promise, usually looser than the SLO, with defined credits if it is missed. The SLO is set tighter so the team gets warning before the contract is breached. Why it works: the SLO converts into an error budget, the amount of failure you are allowed before the target is missed. Worked example: a 99.9 percent availability SLO over 30 days is 30 times 24 times 60, which is 43,200 minutes, multiplied by 0.1 percent, leaving 43.2 minutes of allowed unavailability. If a failover takes 20 minutes on Monday and 15 minutes on Thursday, 35 minutes are spent and about 8 minutes remain. The burn rate, meaning how fast the budget is being spent compared with plan, should drive alerts: spending the whole budget in two days is an urgent page, while spending it at a steady pace is a ticket. Common mistake: measuring the SLI only on the database server. A server can report healthy while clients time out because of connection limits or network paths, so measure at or near the client. Consequence: when the error budget is exhausted, a sensible team pauses risky schema changes and non-urgent maintenance until the budget recovers, which is why these numbers belong in planning, not only in reports.

questions.prompt: A ticket-routing service stores its data in a managed relational database. Its availability SLO is 99.95 percent over a 28-day window. Step 1: the window is 28 times 24 times 60, which is 40,320 minutes. Step 2 (missing, and you must supply it): the allowed failure is 0.05 percent of the window, so the error budget is 40,320 times 0.0005, which equals 20.16 minutes. Two outages then occur: one of 9 minutes and one of 7 minutes, so 16 minutes are spent. How many minutes of error budget remain?
choices: 20.16 minutes remain
36.16 minutes remain
4.16 minutes remain
16.00 minutes remain
questions.why: The budget is 20.16 minutes and 16 minutes are spent, so 20.16 minus 16 leaves 4.16 minutes, which is the remaining budget.

questions.prompt: A reporting team has promised a customer 99 percent monthly uptime, with service credits if that promise is missed. Internally, the team aims for 99.5 percent uptime each month. Which of these is the SLO?
choices: The leftover minutes of allowed downtime, because the team tracks them
The 99 percent customer promise, because it carries service credits
The 99.5 percent internal target, because it is set tighter than the external promise
The ratio of successful reads to total reads, because it is the measurement itself
questions.why: The SLO is the internal target over a window, and the external promise with credits is the SLA, which is usually looser than the SLO.

questions.prompt: A team's database server dashboard shows that 100 percent of queries finish within 150 milliseconds, yet customers report frequent timeouts when connecting. The server metrics are accurate. What is the most likely reason the measurement misses the problem, and what should the team change?
choices: The error budget is being spent too slowly, so the team should raise the burn rate
The window is too long, so the team should shorten it to one day
The SLO is too tight, so the team should loosen it to 99 percent
The measurement is taken only on the server, so the team should measure at or near the client
questions.why: A server can report healthy while clients time out because of connection limits or network paths, so the SLI must be measured at or near the client.

questions.prompt: A team has a 99.9 percent availability SLO over a rolling 7-day window. The window contains 10,080 minutes, so the error budget is 10.08 minutes. Two days into the window, the team has already spent 9 minutes of that budget. How should the team respond to the alert?
choices: Open a ticket for later review, because the team still has about 1 minute left
Ignore it until the window ends, because the budget resets at the end of each week
Pause all monitoring, because a high burn rate means the measurement is wrong
Treat it as an urgent page, because the budget is being spent far faster than a steady pace
questions.why: Spending most of the budget in the first two days of a seven-day window is a fast burn rate, which the teaching text says should trigger an urgent page rather than a ticket.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only ever watched a dashboard the difference between an SLA, an SLO and an SLI, and why we alert on how fast the error budget is being used rather than on every single slow query. Name one limit or tradeoff of setting a very tight target.
lessons.modelAnswer: An SLI is the measurement itself, such as the share of database queries answered in under 200 milliseconds, measured from the client side. The SLO is our internal target for that measurement over a window, say 99.9 percent over 30 days. The SLA is the customer-facing promise, looser than the SLO, with credits if it is broken, so we have margin to act before we breach it. We alert on burn rate instead of individual slow queries because one slow query is normal noise, while burning the error budget quickly signals a real problem that will exhaust the allowance. The tradeoff of a tight target is that each extra nine of availability costs real money and engineering effort, and it leaves less room for planned maintenance, so teams often accept a slightly looser SLO that still matches what users need.
rubricPoints: An SLI is a measured ratio of good events to total events, taken from the user's side.
An SLO is an internal target for an SLI over a time window, set tighter than the external SLA.
The SLA is the contractual promise with consequences such as credits if missed.
Alerting on error budget burn rate catches real trends while ignoring normal single-event noise, and a tight target costs money and leaves less room for maintenance.

suggested.rationale: Turning an SLO into a burn-rate alert is a metric alarm exercise that the planned alarm-builder engine would let the learner practise directly.

lessons.plain: Moving a database from one place to another while the application keeps running is like moving a shop to a new building. You can close the doors for a weekend and carry everything across, or you can keep trading while a copy follows you, catching every sale as it happens, and only switch the sign on the door once the new shop is fully caught up. The right choice depends on how long customers can wait. This objective is about picking the approach that fits a database's downtime tolerance, planning the exact moment you switch over, and keeping a way back to the old building if the new one misbehaves.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retailer's order database must stay writable during business hours, but the team can afford a planned maintenance window of a few hours once a month. Before any teaching, which migration approach would you expect to fit each situation, and what is the main thing you would worry about in each?
lessons.teach:
Cutover is the moment you stop sending writes to the old database and start sending them to the new one. A migration strategy is mostly a decision about how much change you can tolerate in flight and how long writes can be paused at cutover.

Extended outage (also called offline migration) works like this: you stop application writes, export a consistent copy of the source, import it into the target, verify the copy, and point the application at the target. Downtime lasts as long as the export, transfer, import and verification take. It is simple and cheap, and it fits a maintenance window measured in hours.

Near-zero or zero downtime (online migration) works differently. First you take a full snapshot of the source while it keeps serving traffic. Then you use change data capture, meaning a process that reads the source's transaction log and streams every later insert, update and delete to the target. The target runs slightly behind, and that gap is called replication lag. At cutover you pause writes briefly, wait until lag reaches zero, verify row counts and checksums, and switch. Downtime is only the pause, often seconds to minutes.

Worked example: a 500 GB database whose owner allows a four-hour window. The export and import take about three hours including verification, so an extended outage fits. If the allowed window were five minutes, the team would snapshot during normal hours, let change capture run for a day until lag sits at zero, pause writes for two minutes, verify, and repoint.

Common mistake: cutting over while lag is small but not zero, or leaving the old database writable. Both accept writes that never reach the other side, so data diverges silently.

Keep the source untouched and read-only until the new system has proven itself. That retained source is your fallback, and the fallback plan states what would trigger a rollback and how long it stays available.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm migrates a 120 GB order database to a new cloud target. Its shipping application can be paused for no more than 10 minutes, so the team chooses an online migration. Their steps so far: (1) they take a full snapshot of the source while it keeps serving orders; (2) they start change data capture, which reads the source's transaction log and streams later inserts, updates and deletes to the target; (3) [MISSING STEP]; (4) they pause order writes for 90 seconds; (5) they verify row counts and checksums, then point the application at the target. Which step fills the gap at position 3?
choices: They wait until replication lag on the target reaches zero before pausing writes.
They allow writes on both databases so orders are accepted during the wait.
They shut down the source database and delete its transaction log to free disk space.
They export a fresh dump of the source and import it into the target from scratch.
questions.why: Before the brief write pause, the target must have caught up fully, so lag has to reach zero; the other options either leave the old and new databases both writable or discard the change stream the migration depends on.

questions.prompt: A bank holds a 300 GB customer ledger. Its owner has agreed to a single planned outage of up to six hours on a Sunday, and the team wants the simplest, cheapest approach with no change streaming. Which strategy fits?
choices: Near-zero migration with a snapshot followed by a short write pause
Dual-write migration where the application writes to old and new databases at once
Extended outage migration: stop writes, export, import, verify, then repoint
Zero-downtime online migration using change data capture from the transaction log
questions.why: An extended outage fits when the allowed pause is measured in hours, because downtime simply covers the export, transfer, import and verification, with no need to stream later changes.

questions.prompt: A team cuts over a ticketing database while its replication lag is about 3 seconds, not zero, and leaves the old database accepting writes as a precaution. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The new database slows down until the lag clears on its own.
The change capture process automatically rolls the old database back to its snapshot.
Nothing visible happens because a 3-second gap is too small to matter for row counts.
Writes accepted by the old database never reach the new one, so the two copies silently diverge.
questions.why: Cutting over with lag above zero while the old system stays writable means some accepted writes are never copied across, and nothing alerts the team, so the data drifts apart silently.

questions.prompt: After a successful cutover of a retail inventory database, the team wants a safe fallback in case the new system fails in its first month. Which plan best matches sound migration practice?
choices: Keep the source writable so either system can take orders at any time.
Keep the source untouched and read-only, and write down what would trigger a rollback and how long the source stays available.
Delete the source once verification passes, since the copy on the target is now authoritative.
Keep the source running as the active backup until the new system is fully proven, with no stated rollback triggers.
questions.why: The retained, read-only source is the fallback, and the plan should state both the rollback trigger and the period the source remains available, so the fallback is deliberate rather than improvised.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between an extended-outage migration and a near-zero-downtime migration for a production database. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the downtime the business will accept, measured in minutes or hours, and from the database size, since that sets how long a full copy takes. If the window covers the full export, transfer and import, an extended outage is simpler and has fewer moving parts. If not, I use a snapshot followed by continuous change capture, so the target stays close to the source. The cost of that approach is operational: the replication job must keep up with write volume, lag must be watched, and the source's transaction log must be retained long enough for the job to read it. Continuous replication also does not remove the need for verification or a fallback plan. I would still keep the source intact and read-only for a defined period after cutover, so that a rollback is possible if the target misbehaves.
rubricPoints: Downtime tolerance and data size together determine whether an offline or online approach fits.
Online migration uses a full snapshot plus continuous change capture, with downtime limited to the cutover pause.
Cutover requires writes to be paused and replication lag to reach zero before switching, followed by verification.
The source database is kept intact as a fallback, with a defined rollback trigger and retention period.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a strategy from a downtime budget is best learned by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, and no listed mission covers database migration.

lessons.plain: Imagine moving a busy shop into a new building. You open the new shop, move customers over, but keep the old building ready in case the new one runs into trouble. Reverse replication is the process of copying every new sale made in the new building back into the old one, so the old building stays up to date. If you need to go back, the old system already has the latest information instead of a stale copy. It works as a safety net during a move, but only if everyone agrees on which building is accepting new customers at any given time.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have moved your application's writes to a new database and it has been running for a day. Before you decide to switch back to the old database, what would you expect to be true about the old database, and why?
lessons.teach:
Replication means continuously copying changes from one database to another, so the second copy stays close to the first. In a migration, the original database is the source and the new database is the target. Cutover is the moment you point the application at the target and stop using the source for writes. Fallback is the plan for returning to the source if the target misbehaves after cutover. Reverse replication is the technique that makes fallback realistic: after cutover, every change committed on the new target is streamed back to the old source. Without it, the source stops receiving changes the moment you cut over, so rolling back would mean losing everything written since then or doing a painful manual reconciliation.

Why it works: the replication tool reads the change log of the database that is accepting writes and applies those changes to the other side, the same way it did in the forward direction, only reversed. Worked example: the source holds 10,000 orders. At 09:00 you cut over and the target accepts 300 new orders. Reverse replication sends those 300 inserts back to the source as they commit. At 11:00 a serious bug appears on the target. Because the source already holds the 300 orders, you can point the application back at it with only a short delay in lag.

Common mistake: assuming reverse replication keeps two writable databases in sync. If the application writes to both sides, the copies diverge and the tool may fail or silently produce conflicting rows. Only one side should accept writes at a time.

Consequence: if writes are allowed on the source while reverse replication is running from the target, you have created a split situation that is hard to repair safely. Reverse replication is a fallback path, not a second primary.

questions.prompt: A records company runs an invoice database on a server in its own data centre (the source). At 14:00 it cuts over to a managed cloud database (the target). Reverse replication, the process that streams each committed change from the target back to the source, runs from cutover onward. The target accepts 120 new invoices. At 16:30 a fault is found on the target. Step 1: the team stops new writes to the target. Step 2: they wait until reverse replication lag reaches zero and confirm the source holds all 120 invoices. Step 3 is missing. Which action completes the fallback?
choices: Delete the 120 invoices from the target to avoid duplicate rows
Turn writes back on at the target so customers see no gap
Point the app at the old server; make the target read-only
Turn on writes on both servers so the application can pick either
questions.why: Once the source has every committed change, the application is pointed at it and the target is made read-only so only one side accepts writes, which is the rule that keeps fallback safe.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does reverse replication do during a fallback plan?
choices: It deletes the source's old rows once the target is trusted
It converts the target's data into the source's file format once
It copies the target's committed changes back to the source as they happen
It pauses the target so the source can take the next write
questions.why: Reverse replication streams changes committed on the new target back to the old source continuously, so the source stays current enough to fall back to.

questions.prompt: A shipping firm cut over to a new cloud database at 06:00. Reverse replication was not set up. By 08:00 the target had taken 45 shipment status updates, and then a bug forced a rollback to the old server. What is the most accurate consequence?
choices: The 45 updates are kept automatically because the target retains them
The source has no record of the 45 updates unless someone reconciles by hand
The source applies the 45 updates on its own once it is restarted
Nothing is lost because the source keeps a copy of every write request
questions.why: Without reverse replication the source stops receiving changes at cutover, so the 45 updates exist only on the target and must be recovered through a manual, error-prone reconciliation.

questions.prompt: A team has reverse replication running from the new target back to the old source. A developer, unaware of the plan, keeps the application writing to both databases during the fallback window. What is the most likely result?
choices: The tool merges both sets of writes into one correct copy automatically
The target stops accepting writes until the source is turned off
The copies diverge and the tool may fail or silently produce conflicting rows
Reverse replication speeds up because there is less data to move
questions.why: Reverse replication assumes only one side accepts writes; writes on both sides make the copies diverge, causing failures or conflicting rows.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what reverse replication is, why a team would switch it on after cutover, and name one limit or tradeoff they must watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Reverse replication copies changes made on the new database back to the original one after we have moved our application over. We set it up so the old database stays current, which means if the new system has a serious problem we can switch back without losing the orders written in the meantime. The key tradeoff is that only one side should accept writes at a time. If the application still writes to the old database while changes are flowing back from the new one, the two copies can diverge and conflict, and untangling that is slow and risky. Another limit is lag: the old side is only as current as the last change it has received, so a fallback decision needs to account for that small gap. We also have to remember that the reverse path only carries what the replication tool can capture, so schema changes made on the new side may need to be applied to the old side by hand. Fallback is possible only while the reverse stream is healthy, so we should verify it regularly rather than assume it works.
rubricPoints: Defines reverse replication as copying changes from the new target back to the original source after cutover
States that its purpose is to keep the source current so fallback loses no recent writes
Names the key limit: only one side may accept writes, or the copies diverge
Mentions replication lag or that schema changes may not flow automatically

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining the fallback tradeoff in your own words, which no listed mission or planned engine currently drills.

lessons.plain: A database migration is moving a database from where it runs today to a new home while the application keeps working. Planning it means deciding in advance what gets moved, how the structure and queries are translated into the new database's language, when the switch happens, and how you would step back if the new system misbehaves. Think of moving house: you list what goes in the van, check that your appliances fit the new kitchen, pick a moving day, and keep the old place's keys until you are sure you will not need to go back. The fallback plan is those keys.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team copies all the data from an old database to a new one over the weekend and switches the app to it on Monday. The copy finishes and the row counts match on both sides. Name one thing that could still be wrong after Monday that a row count would not catch.
lessons.teach:
DDL (data definition language) is the set of statements that describe structure: creating tables, columns, data types, indexes and constraints. DML (data manipulation language) is the set that reads and changes rows: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. Converting means rewriting both so they run on the target database, which often uses different type names, functions and rules. A cutover is the moment the application starts writing to the new database. A fallback plan is a tested way to send traffic back to the old database if the new one fails, together with written criteria for when to trigger it.

The reason to plan this way is that the database holds data that usually cannot be recreated, so every step must answer 'what if we need to stop here?'

Worked example. The source has an amount column declared as a 10-digit whole number and a report query that uses NVL(discount, 0) to replace missing discounts with zero. Step 1: inventory every table, view and query the application uses. Step 2: convert the DDL, mapping the number type to a target integer type and checking that the value range fits. Step 3: convert the DML, rewriting NVL(discount, 0) as COALESCE(discount, 0), which gives the same answer here. Step 4: load a copy and compare the results of the most important queries, not just row counts. Step 5: write down the cutover window, the rollback trigger (for example, error rate above an agreed level for 15 minutes) and the reverse path. Step 6: rehearse the rollback before the real day.

Common mistake: treating matching row counts as proof that the migration works. Two databases can hold the same rows yet handle NULLs, time zones, text case or integer division differently, so a report can change silently.

Consequence: if you cut over without a tested fallback and find a problem on day three, returning to the old database loses every write made since cutover, unless those writes were copied back.

questions.prompt: A regional bus operator is moving its ticket database to a new cloud database. Its fare table stores price as a 9-digit whole number of cents, and a sales report uses IFNULL(refund, 0) to treat missing refunds as zero, which the target database spells COALESCE(refund, 0). Worked so far: Step 1, the team listed every table, view and query the app uses. Step 2, the fare price column was mapped to a 64-bit integer type after confirming the values fit. Step 3, the IFNULL report query was rewritten as COALESCE(refund, 0). Step 4 is missing from the notes. Step 5, the team wrote the cutover window, the rollback trigger (checkout error rate above 2 percent for 10 minutes) and the reverse path. Which step belongs in the gap between Step 3 and Step 5?
choices: Load a copy into the target and compare the results of the key sales queries, not just the row counts
Skip rehearsing the rollback because Steps 1 to 3 already cover the risk
Rename the fare table to match the name used by the old reporting tool
Drop the secondary indexes on the fare table so the load runs faster
questions.why: Loading a copy and comparing query results is the verification step that tests whether the converted DDL and DML give the same answers, and it must come before writing the cutover plan.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, which statement correctly separates DDL from DML?
choices: DDL changes rows using INSERT and DELETE, while DML creates tables and indexes
DDL covers only SELECT queries, while DML covers only the statements that create indexes
DDL describes structure such as tables, columns, types, indexes and constraints, while DML reads and changes rows using SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
DDL and DML are two names for the same set of statements, used on different vendors' databases
questions.why: The teaching text defines DDL as structure-describing statements and DML as row-reading and row-changing statements, and only the first choice matches that split.

questions.prompt: A team migrating a customer database finds that the row count in the new database matches the old one exactly. A colleague says this proves the migration worked. What is the best response?
choices: Agree, because matching counts means every row was copied with the right values
Agree only if the table has no indexes, since indexes can change row counts
Ask for a rollback rehearsal instead, since counts never matter after cutover
Disagree, because two databases with the same rows can still treat NULLs, time zones, text case or integer division differently, so key query results must also be compared
questions.why: The teaching text states that matching row counts do not prove correctness, because the two databases can handle NULLs, time zones, text case and integer division differently.

questions.prompt: A retail team cut over to the new database on Monday. On Wednesday they find a conversion error and decide to return to the old database. Which preparation was needed so that Tuesday's orders are not lost?
choices: Only the row-count comparison from before cutover, because it proves the old data is complete
A rollback trigger of 15 minutes, which automatically keeps new writes in both databases
A restore of the old database from the backup taken on Sunday, because that keeps all writes
A tested reverse path that copies every write made since cutover back to the old database
questions.why: Without a tested reverse path that copies post-cutover writes back, returning to the old database loses those writes, and restoring a pre-cutover backup would discard them, so the reverse path is the required preparation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only run small local databases why a migration plan needs both a fallback plan and a DDL/DML conversion step. Name one limit of automatic conversion that the plan must still test.
lessons.modelAnswer: A migration is a one-way door unless we plan for coming back. Once the application writes to the new database, the old one falls behind, so the fallback plan says when we would switch back, how we would test that the old system still works, and how writes made after cutover would be handled. Conversion is needed because the two databases do not speak the same dialect. The table structure, the data types and the queries all have to be rewritten, or the application will fail or behave differently. The limit is that a converter can rewrite syntax but cannot know intent. A function may exist on both sides yet treat NULLs, rounding or time zones differently, so the plan must include comparing real query results between the two databases, not just checking that the statements run without errors.
rubricPoints: A fallback plan lets the team return to the old database if the new one fails, and needs clear trigger criteria.
DDL defines structure and DML reads and changes rows; both must be converted for the target database.
Automatic conversion rewrites syntax but cannot guarantee the same behaviour for every function or type.
Matching row counts is not enough; important query results should be compared between source and target.
Writes made after cutover are lost on rollback unless they are copied back, so the fallback must account for them.

suggested.rationale: Translating a source table definition and its queries into a target dialect and comparing results is the practice this objective needs, and the planned SQL lab would let learners do it directly.

lessons.plain: When a company moves a database from its own machines or another cloud into Google Cloud, the data has to travel and the application has to switch over to the new copy. Choosing a migration tool means picking the helper that moves the data in a way that fits how long the business can accept the database being unavailable. Some approaches copy a snapshot and accept a planned pause while it loads. Others keep copying changes as they happen, so the final switch takes only seconds. Think of moving house: you can pack everything and wait a weekend, or you can move the most recent boxes continuously until the last load is small. This lesson is about matching the tool to the situation before any work starts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank's customer database runs in a data centre and can be offline for no more than a few seconds per month. Would you copy it once over a weekend and then switch, or copy it once and then keep copying new changes until the switch? Why?
lessons.teach: Source means the database you are moving from, and target means the database you are moving to. Cutover is the moment applications stop using the source and start using the target. Downtime is the time during which the database cannot serve its normal writes. A dump-and-load approach exports a consistent snapshot of the source and imports it into the target. It is simple and cheap, but the target is only as fresh as the moment the snapshot was taken, so the source must be frozen for the whole copy. Continuous replication, sometimes called change data capture, first loads a snapshot and then reads the source's change log so that every insert, update and delete is replayed on the target. The target stays close behind the source, and cutover only needs to wait for the last few changes to apply. Worked example: a 2 TB MySQL database on premises can tolerate a four hour window on Sunday night. A one-time export and import is estimated at three hours, so the dump-and-load approach fits. Change the requirement so payments can stop for under five minutes. Start a continuous migration job, let the initial copy run while the source keeps taking writes, watch the lag fall to near zero, then stop writes on the source, wait for lag to reach zero, promote the target and repoint applications. Common mistake: choosing a tool by data size alone, or assuming cutover is instant without freezing writes on the source. Consequence in a running system: writes that land on the source after the lag check are lost or split across two databases. Also confirm that the tool supports your exact source engine, version and target pair, because support changes over time. The tool must match the downtime tolerance.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs a 900 GB PostgreSQL database on a rented server outside Google Cloud. Its business can tolerate about 12 minutes of write downtime. The team has chosen continuous replication, which loads a snapshot and then replays later changes from the source's change log onto the target. They work through the steps in order. Step 1: confirm the migration tool supports their exact source engine, version and target pair. Step 2: start the job so the initial copy runs while the source keeps taking writes. Step 3: watch the lag fall to near zero. Step 4 is missing from their notes. What should it be?
choices: Freeze writes on the source, wait for lag to reach zero, then promote the target and repoint applications.
Delete the source database once the initial copy completes, so applications cannot write to it by mistake.
Promote the target right away, because lag was already near zero when the copy finished.
Run a fresh dump of the source and import it into the target before cutover, since the snapshot is the only consistent copy.
questions.why: Cutover needs writes frozen on the source and lag confirmed at zero before the target is promoted, otherwise late writes are lost or split across two databases.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does continuous replication add that a dump-and-load approach does not?
choices: It makes the copy finish faster because the source is read in parallel across many machines.
It removes the need to check that the target supports the source engine and version.
It replays every later insert, update and delete from the source's change log onto the target after the snapshot, so the target stays close behind.
It keeps the source frozen during the whole copy, so no writes can be lost.
questions.why: Continuous replication loads a snapshot and then applies later changes from the change log, which keeps the target near the source's current state.

questions.prompt: A reporting team has a 300 GB source database hosted outside Google Cloud. The business accepts a 9-hour outage on Saturday night, and a one-time export and import is estimated to take 5 hours. Which approach fits, and why?
choices: Dump-and-load, because the estimated copy fits inside the accepted window and the approach is simple and cheap.
Continuous replication, because it avoids any downtime, so it is always the safer choice even when the window is generous.
Dump-and-load, but only if the source keeps taking writes during the export so the target stays fresh.
Continuous replication, because any database over 100 GB must use change data capture regardless of the window.
questions.why: The tool must match the downtime tolerance; a 5-hour copy fits a 9-hour window, so the simpler and cheaper dump-and-load approach is appropriate.

questions.prompt: A team's lag check showed zero at 14:00. They promoted the target at 14:02, but the application kept writing to the source for two more minutes because a configuration file had not been updated, and the source was never frozen. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The source refuses writes once a promotion starts, so the application gets errors but no data is split.
Writes made to the source during those two minutes are lost or split between two databases, because they landed after the lag check.
Nothing: lag was zero at the check, so the target already holds every write.
The target automatically sends those writes back to the source, so no data is lost.
questions.why: Writes that land on the source after the lag check are not replayed onto the target, so they are lost or end up split across two databases.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a one-time dump-and-load and continuous replication when moving an external database into Google Cloud. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the downtime the business will accept, then the database size and the source engine. If the window is long enough to copy the data while the source is frozen, a one-time dump and load is simpler and cheaper, with fewer moving parts. If the window must be minutes or seconds, I use continuous replication: it loads a snapshot, keeps applying the source's changes, and only needs a short final cutover once lag is near zero. The tradeoff of continuous replication is that it needs a supported source configuration, such as change logging enabled, and a steady network connection, and the cutover still has to freeze writes correctly or data is lost. The tradeoff of a one-time dump is that the window grows with data size, so a large database may not finish in time.
rubricPoints: Chooses the approach from the allowed downtime, not from habit
Explains that continuous replication keeps the target near the source and shortens cutover
Explains that a one-time dump requires a frozen source for the whole copy
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff of the approach not chosen first
Notes that the source engine and version must be supported

suggested.rationale: Choosing a migration tool from a downtime requirement is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios that vary the constraints.

lessons.plain: A highly available database is one that keeps answering requests when part of its underlying infrastructure fails, such as one machine or one data center zone. Running on a managed cloud service does not by itself guarantee this; the specific setup decides it. Think of a shop with two cashiers in different rooms: if one room floods, the other keeps taking payments. In Google Cloud you make this choice when you create the database, by asking for redundancy across zones inside a region so that a standby copy can take over automatically. It is a provisioning decision, made before the system ever runs under load.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your production database runs on a single virtual machine in one zone, with nightly backups. A zone outage happens at 14:00. What do you expect users to experience, and what setup change would most reduce that impact?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A zone is an isolated data center inside a region, which is a geographic area containing several zones. High availability (HA) means the database keeps serving requests after a component fails, so that a single failure costs only a short interruption. Redundancy means keeping a second copy of the data and a second way to run it. A standby is a second instance that stays ready to take over. Failover is the switch from a failed primary instance to the standby. Synchronous replication means each write is confirmed on both copies before the application is told it succeeded, so the standby never lacks a committed write. A backup is a saved copy of the data taken at a point in time, used for restoring.

Why it works: when you provision a regional HA configuration, the service places the primary in one zone and a standby in another zone of the same region, and keeps their storage in step. If the primary's zone fails, the service promotes the standby and the database keeps the same connection name, so applications reconnect rather than being reconfigured. Failover is not instant: clients see errors and a pause for the duration of a restart, and open connections are dropped.

Worked example. A dispatch database is created as a single zonal instance. Zone A fails. There is no standby, so the team restores the last backup into a new instance, repoints every application, and accepts the writes made since that backup are gone. Now create the same database with regional HA: primary in zone A, standby in zone B, synchronous replication between them. Zone A fails, the standby is promoted, applications reconnect within minutes, and no committed write is lost.

Common mistake: treating backups as high availability. Backups protect against corruption and accidental deletion; they do not keep the service running during an outage. A standby in the same zone also fails together with that zone.

Consequence: zone-level HA protects against a zone failure but not a full regional outage, which needs cross-region replication or a disaster-recovery plan, both separate topics.

High availability is set when the database is provisioned, and placing the standby in a different zone is what makes it real.

questions.prompt: A payroll company, Brightwater Payroll, creates its payroll database in region europe-west1 using the regional high availability option. Step 1: the primary instance is placed in zone europe-west1-b. Step 2: each committed write is synchronously replicated to a standby. Step 3: the standby is placed in ______, so that an outage of zone europe-west1-b leaves a running copy to take over.
choices: a nightly backup file in Cloud Storage, which is kept ready to be promoted to primary
the same zone, europe-west1-b, because keeping both copies together gives the lowest replication latency
a different zone within europe-west1, such as europe-west1-c, so a single zone failure cannot take down both copies
a different region, such as europe-north1, because that is what protects against a zone failure
questions.why: Regional high availability places the standby in a different zone of the same region, which is what lets it survive the failure of the primary's zone.

questions.prompt: A clinic books appointments in a single zonal database instance in one zone. Which change most directly makes the service keep running if that one zone fails?
choices: Take backups every hour instead of every day
Add a read-only copy in the same zone as the primary
Recreate the database with regional high availability, so a standby exists in a different zone of the same region
Increase the machine size of the instance so it can handle more requests
questions.why: Only a standby in another zone, set up at provisioning time, lets the service keep serving after the primary's zone fails; the other options do not add a second zone.

questions.prompt: A grain company, Harvest Grain, runs its primary database and its standby both in zone us-central1-a. That zone suffers an outage. What is the most likely result?
choices: Both copies are unavailable together, because a standby in the same zone fails along with that zone
Writes are queued in backups until the zone recovers
Only the primary is unavailable, and the standby keeps accepting writes
The standby is promoted automatically and clients see no errors at all
questions.why: A standby in the same zone shares the zone's failure, so it cannot take over, which is why the standby must sit in a different zone to provide high availability.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm, Coastline Freight, takes hourly backups of its shipment database. Yesterday a faulty script deleted a set of rows, and separately a zone outage is now causing downtime. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Backups cannot be used for restoring because they are only a copy of the standby
Backups let the firm restore data removed by the faulty script, but they do not keep the service running during the zone outage
The hourly backups keep the database running through the zone outage, so no downtime occurs
Because backups exist, the firm does not need any high availability configuration at all
questions.why: Backups protect against deletion and corruption by restoring earlier data, but they do not keep the service running during an outage, which needs a standby set up in advance.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our database is highly available because it is a managed service with backups turned on. Explain to them, in your own words, what specifically makes a database highly available when you provision it, and name one limit that remains even with that setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: Managed hosting alone does not make a database highly available. What matters is the provisioning choice: the database is created with a standby copy in a different zone of the same region, and writes are synchronously replicated so a committed write exists on both copies. If the primary's zone fails, the service fails over to the standby and keeps the same connection name, so the application reconnects. Backups are a different thing. They let us restore after corruption or deletion, but restoring takes far longer and can lose recent writes. The limit is that failover is not instant. Clients see errors and a short pause, and in-flight transactions are interrupted, so the application has to retry safely. Also, this covers a zone failure, not a whole-region outage, which needs a separate disaster-recovery plan.
rubricPoints: High availability comes from a standby in a different zone of the same region, chosen when the database is created.
Synchronous replication means a committed write exists on both copies before success is reported.
Failover promotes the standby and keeps the connection name, but it is not instant and drops open connections.
Backups are not high availability; they restore data but do not keep the service running.
Zone-level high availability does not cover a full regional outage.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining what specifically makes a database highly available and naming its limits, which is best practised by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: Testing high availability and disaster recovery means checking, on purpose and before a real problem, that a database keeps working when part of it fails and that you can recover data after a serious loss. High availability is about staying up through smaller failures, such as one machine or one data center zone going down. Disaster recovery is about getting back after a bigger event, such as a region outage or a mistaken delete. A plan written on paper is not proof. The only way to know the switch works and fits your time limits is to break things in a controlled way and measure what happens.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team says the database is highly available because it has a standby copy in another zone. What single test would you run to find out whether that claim is actually true, and what would you measure?
lessons.teach:
Testing here means running a planned experiment against a database to see whether its failover and recovery behave as promised. Two numbers frame the work. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the service may be unavailable after a failure. The recovery point objective (RPO) is how much recent data you may lose, measured as the time between the last safely confirmed write and the failure. A design is only as good as its ability to meet both numbers under realistic conditions.

Why it works: a standby or replica only helps if it can take over quickly and holds the data you think it does. Replication is often asynchronous, so the standby may trail the primary by some seconds.
